ra_g1_01.title: The Red Hat
ra_g1_01.text: Sam has a red hat. The wind is strong today. It lifts the hat off his head and drops it in a big puddle! Sam picks it up and laughs.

q.text: What color is the hat?
q.why: The first line: "Sam has a red hat."

q.text: What took the hat?
q.why: "The wind is strong today. It lifts the hat off his head."

q.text: How does Sam feel at the end?
q.why: "Sam picks it up and laughs." You laugh when you are glad, not mad or sad.

ra_g1_02.title: Drip, Drop
ra_g1_02.text:
Drip, drop, rain on the roof.
Drip, drop, rain on the street.
Puddles, puddles, all around,
Splash them with your feet!
Then the sun comes out to play.

q.text: Where is the rain at the start?
q.why: The first line: "rain on the roof."

q.text: What do you splash?
q.why: "Puddles, puddles, all around, / Splash them with your feet!"

q.text: What comes out at the end?
q.why: The last line: "Then the sun comes out to play."

ra_g1_03.title: The Big Box
ra_g1_03.text: Dad got a new lamp in a big box. Ben and Kim did not care about the lamp. They wanted the box! They cut a door and a window in it. Now it is their fort.

q.text: What did the kids want?
q.why: "Ben and Kim did not care about the lamp. They wanted the box!"

q.text: Why did they cut a door?
q.why: They made a fort. You go in and out of a fort by a door.

q.text: What is the best name for this?
q.why: The kids turn the box into a fort. The lamp is only how the box got there.

ra_g1_04.title: The Lost Mitten
ra_g1_04.text: Mia lost a mitten in the snow. She looked by the tree. She looked by the swing. Then her dog ran up with something in his mouth. It was the mitten!

q.text: Who found the mitten?
q.why: "Her dog ran up with something in his mouth. It was the mitten!"

q.text: Why did Mia look by the swing?
q.why: The story starts "Mia lost a mitten," and then she looks for it.

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: Mia loses her mitten and gets it back. The dog was not lost.

ra_g1_05.title: The Moon
ra_g1_05.text: The moon does not make its own light. The light we see comes from the sun. There is no wind or rain on the moon. A footprint there can stay for a very long time.

q.text: Where does the moon get its light?
q.why: "The light we see comes from the sun."

q.text: Why can a footprint stay there?
c: No wind or rain wipes it.
q.why: "There is no wind or rain on the moon. A footprint there can stay for a very long time."

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: Each line tells something about the moon.

ra_g1_06.title: A Note from Gran
ra_g1_06.text:
Dear Pat,
Thank you for the picture of the cat you drew. I put it on my fridge. It makes me smile every day. Come and see my new kittens soon!
Love, Gran

q.text: What did Pat send?
q.why: "Thank you for the picture of the cat you drew."

q.text: Where is it now?
q.why: "I put it on my fridge."

q.text: Does Gran like it?
q.why: "It makes me smile every day."

ra_g1_07.title: Night Hunters
ra_g1_07.text: Most owls hunt at night. Big eyes help them see in the dark. Soft feathers let them fly with almost no sound. A mouse may not hear an owl coming!

q.text: When do most owls hunt?
q.why: The first line: "Most owls hunt at night."

q.text: What helps an owl fly with no sound?
q.why: "Soft feathers let them fly with almost no sound."

q.text: Why does no sound help an owl?
c: It can sing to the mouse.
The mouse does not hear it.
q.why: "A mouse may not hear an owl coming!" — so the owl can catch it.

ra_g1_08.title: Jen's Bean
ra_g1_08.text: Jen put a bean seed in a cup of dirt. Each day she gave it a little water. One morning she saw a tiny green sprout, no bigger than her fingernail. She set the cup in the sun by the window.

q.text: What did Jen give it each day?
q.why: "Each day she gave it a little water."

q.text: What does tiny mean?
q.why: The sprout was "no bigger than her fingernail" — very small.

q.text: Why is the cup by the window?
q.why: "She set the cup in the sun by the window." Plants need sun to grow.

ra_g1_09.title: Busy Bees
ra_g1_09.text: Honey bees fly from flower to flower. They drink a sweet juice called nectar. They take it back to the hive. There they turn it into honey to eat in the winter.

q.text: What is nectar?
q.why: "They drink a sweet juice called nectar."

q.text: Where do the bees take it?
q.why: "They take it back to the hive."

q.text: When do bees eat the honey?
q.why: "They turn it into honey to eat in the winter."

ra_g1_10.title: From Egg to Frog
ra_g1_10.text: A frog starts as a tiny egg in a pond. The egg hatches into a tadpole with a long tail. The tadpole swims and grows legs. Then its tail is gone, and it can hop out of the pond!

q.text: What is a frog at the start?
q.why: "A frog starts as a tiny egg in a pond." The tadpole comes next.

q.text: What does the tadpole get?
q.why: "The tadpole swims and grows legs."

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: Each line tells the next step: egg, tadpole, legs, frog.

ra_g1_11.title: A Snake Gets New Skin
ra_g1_11.text: A snake grows, but its skin does not. So the snake rubs its nose on a rock. The old skin peels off like a sock. Now the snake has new, shiny skin!

q.text: What does the snake rub its nose on?
q.why: "So the snake rubs its nose on a rock."

q.text: The old skin comes off like what?
q.why: "The old skin peels off like a sock."

q.text: What is this about?
c: a snake that eats a lot
q.why: The snake's skin is too small, the old skin comes off, and there is new skin.

ra_g1_12.title: How a Snake Smells
ra_g1_12.text: A snake flicks its tongue in and out. It is not being rude! The tongue picks up smells from the air. That is how a snake finds its food.

q.text: What does the snake flick?
q.why: "A snake flicks its tongue in and out."

q.text: Is the snake being rude?
q.why: "It is not being rude! The tongue picks up smells from the air."

q.text: What does the tongue help it find?
q.why: "That is how a snake finds its food."

ra_g1_13.title: Dinosaur Bones
ra_g1_13.text: Dinosaurs lived long, long ago. No person ever saw one. We know about them from bones in rocks. The bones are called fossils.

q.text: What are fossils?
q.why: "We know about them from bones in rocks. The bones are called fossils."

q.text: Did a person ever see a dinosaur?
q.why: "No person ever saw one."

q.text: What is this about?
c: how to dig a big hole
q.why: We know about dinosaurs, which no one saw, from their bones in rocks.

ra_g1_14.title: Big and Small Dinosaurs
ra_g1_14.text: Some dinosaurs were as big as a house, and some were as small as a hen. Some ate plants, and some ate meat. All of them hatched from eggs.

q.text: How small were some dinosaurs?
q.why: "Some were as small as a hen" — that is the smallest size it gives.

q.text: What did all of them hatch from?
q.why: "All of them hatched from eggs."

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: It tells about big ones, small ones, plant-eaters and meat-eaters.

ra_g1_15.title: Frogs Drink with Skin
ra_g1_15.text: A frog does not drink with its mouth. It soaks up water with its skin! That is why frogs like wet spots. A frog in a dry spot will hop off to find a pond.

q.text: How does a frog drink?
q.why: "It soaks up water with its skin!"

q.text: Why do frogs like wet spots?
q.why: "It soaks up water with its skin! That is why frogs like wet spots."

q.text: Where will a dry frog go?
q.why: "A frog in a dry spot will hop off to find a pond."

ra_g1_16.title: Sticky Toes
ra_g1_16.text: A tree frog can climb up a wall. Its toes are sticky. They help it hold on to wet leaves and glass. It can even sit on a window!

q.text: What helps a tree frog climb?
q.why: "Its toes are sticky. They help it hold on."

q.text: Can a tree frog sit on glass?
q.why: "They help it hold on to wet leaves and glass. It can even sit on a window!"

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: Every line is about the tree frog's sticky toes and climbing.

ra_g1_17.title: The Red Bird
ra_g1_17.text: The cardinal is the state bird of North Carolina. The dad bird is bright red. The mom bird is tan with a bit of red. You can see them all year, even in the snow.

q.text: What color is the dad bird?
q.why: "The dad bird is bright red." The mom bird is tan.

q.text: When can you see them?
q.why: "You can see them all year, even in the snow."

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: Every line is about the cardinal bird.

ra_g1_18.title: Wild Ponies
ra_g1_18.text: Wild horses live on some islands by the sea in North Carolina. They run free, and no one rides them. They eat grass and drink from ponds. People must stay back and let them be.

q.text: Where do the horses live?
q.why: "Wild horses live on some islands by the sea in North Carolina."

q.text: What do they eat?
q.why: "They eat grass and drink from ponds."

q.text: Why must people stay back?
q.why: They are "wild horses" that "run free," so people "let them be."

ra_g1_19.title: Turtle Eggs in the Sand
ra_g1_19.text: In summer, a big sea turtle crawls up on a beach in North Carolina. She digs a hole in the sand. She lays her eggs and covers them up. Then she goes back to the sea.

q.text: Where does she dig a hole?
q.why: "She digs a hole in the sand."

q.text: Does the mom stay with the eggs?
c: No, she goes back to the sea.
Yes, she naps on the beach.
q.why: "Then she goes back to the sea."

q.text: What is this about?
c: a fun day at the beach
q.why: She crawls up, digs, lays her eggs, covers them, and goes back.

ra_g1_20.title: The Muddy Dog
ra_g1_20.text: Rex jumped in the mud, and then he ran into the house! Tim got a tub of water and some soap. Now Rex is clean, but Tim is all wet.

q.text: Where did Rex jump?
q.why: The story starts: "Rex jumped in the mud."

q.text: What did Tim get?
q.why: "Tim got a tub of water and some soap."

q.text: Why is Tim wet?
q.why: He got "a tub of water and some soap," and now Rex is clean — Tim got wet giving the bath.

ra_g1_21.title: The Wiggly Tooth
ra_g1_21.text: Ana had a loose tooth. It went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. At lunch she bit into an apple, and out it came! She put it in a bag to keep it safe.

q.text: What did Ana bite?
q.why: "At lunch she bit into an apple, and out it came!"

q.text: The tooth was loose. What does loose mean?
q.why: It "went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle" — it could move.

q.text: Why did she put it in a bag?
c: so she would not lose it
to give it to a dog
q.why: "She put it in a bag to keep it safe."

ra_g1_22.title: The Snowman
ra_g1_22.text: Max and Dot made a snowman. It had a carrot nose and a red hat. Then the sun came out and got hot. Soon the snowman was just a hat and a carrot in a puddle.

q.text: What was the nose?
q.why: "It had a carrot nose and a red hat."

q.text: What happened to the snowman?
q.why: "The sun came out and got hot," and then it was "a puddle."

q.text: What is the best name for this?
q.why: The snowman is made, then the sun melts it.

ra_g1_23.title: The Sand Castle
ra_g1_23.text: Liz made a sand castle by the sea. A big wave came up. Splash! The castle was gone. Liz just made a new one, a bit farther up.

q.text: What took the castle?
q.why: "A big wave came up. Splash! The castle was gone."

q.text: Why did Liz make the new one farther up?
c: to be close to her mom
so the waves would not get it
to look for shells in the sand
q.why: The wave knocked the first one down, so she moved away from the water.

q.text: How did Liz feel?
c: She was mad and went home.
She was fine and tried again.
q.why: She "just made a new one" — she did not give up.

ra_g1_24.title: The Race to the Gate
ra_g1_24.text: Jake and his dad ran a race all the way to the gate. Dad is big and tall, but Jake is very fast. Jake got to the gate first, and Dad said, "You win!"

q.text: Where did they race to?
q.why: "Jake and his dad ran a race all the way to the gate."

q.text: Who won?
q.why: "Jake got to the gate first, and Dad said, 'You win!'"

q.text: Why did Jake win?
q.why: "Dad is big and tall, but Jake is very fast."

ra_g1_25.title: Three Blue Eggs
ra_g1_25.text: Nell saw a little nest in the bush by her door. In it were three blue eggs, but she did not touch them. She will come back in a week to look for the chicks.

q.text: How many eggs were in the nest?
q.why: "In it were three blue eggs." Not two, not ten.

q.text: What will come out of the eggs?
q.why: She will come back "to look for the chicks."

q.text: Why did Nell not touch the eggs?
q.why: She left them alone so the chicks could hatch. She saw them, so it was not that.

ra_g1_26.title: Flip!
ra_g1_26.text: Dad and Liv made pancakes. Liv mixed, and Dad flipped. One pancake went up and stuck on the wall! They laughed and laughed.

q.text: Who did the mixing?
q.why: "Liv mixed, and Dad flipped."

q.text: Where did one pancake stick?
q.why: "One pancake went up and stuck on the wall!"

q.text: Was it a fun time?
q.why: "They laughed and laughed."

ra_g1_27.title: Little Frog
ra_g1_27.text:
Hop, hop, little frog,
Hop up on the big green log.
Plop, plop, in you go!
Swim so fast, then swim so slow.

q.text: Where does the frog hop?
q.why: "Hop up on the big green log."

q.text: What sound does it make?
q.why: "Plop, plop, in you go!"

q.text: Where is the frog at the end?
q.why: "Plop, plop, in you go! / Swim so fast" — it went in the water to swim.

ra_g1_28.title: Can We Go?
ra_g1_28.text:
Dear Mom,
I fed the fish and made my bed. I put my dirty socks in the bin. Can we go to the park and play on the swings now?
Love, Jack

q.text: What did Jack feed?
q.why: "I fed the fish and made my bed."

q.text: What does Jack want?
q.why: "Can we go to the park and play on the swings now?"

q.text: Why does Jack tell Mom his jobs?
q.why: He lists the jobs he did, then asks to go — his work is done.

ra_g1_29.title: Wash Your Hands
ra_g1_29.text: Get your hands wet. Rub on soap and sing a song. Rub the backs and in between the fingers. Then rinse and dry.

q.text: What do you do first?
q.why: "Get your hands wet." Drying is last.

q.text: What do you rub on?
q.why: "Rub on soap and sing a song."

q.text: What do these steps help you do?
q.why: Wet, soap, rub, rinse, dry — they are the steps to wash your hands.

ra_g1_30.title: The Sun Is a Star
ra_g1_30.text: The sun is a star. It looks big because it is close to us. The other stars are very far away. That is why they look so small at night.

q.text: What is the sun?
q.why: The first line: "The sun is a star."

q.text: Why do the stars look small?
q.why: "The other stars are very far away. That is why they look so small."

q.text: What is this about?
q.why: It tells that the sun is a star and why the stars look small.

ra_g2_01.title: My Friend the Snail
ra_g2_01.text:
A snail goes slowly up the wall.
It carries its house, and that is all.
When rain comes down, it comes out to play.
When the sun is hot, it hides away.
It leaves a shiny, silver trail,
So I can always find my snail.

q.text: What does the snail do when the sun is hot?
q.why: "When the sun is hot, it hides away."

q.text: What is the snail's "house"?
q.why: A snail carries its shell everywhere, so "it carries its house" means its shell.

q.text: How does the poet find the snail?
c: by looking for its shiny trail
q.why: "It leaves a shiny, silver trail, / So I can always find my snail."

ra_g2_02.title: Grace at the Pool
ra_g2_02.text: Grace stood at the edge of the pool. Her legs felt shaky. The teacher smiled and said, "Hold on to the wall and kick." Grace kicked hard and made a big splash. By the end of the lesson, she let go of the wall and floated on her back for five whole seconds.

q.text: How did Grace feel at the start?
q.why: "Her legs felt shaky" while she stood at the edge — she was nervous.

q.text: What did the teacher tell her to do?
c: hold on to the wall and kick
swim to the end of the pool
q.why: "Hold on to the wall and kick."

q.text: How did Grace change during the lesson?
c: She got bored and went home.
She swam across the whole pool.
q.why: At the end "she let go of the wall and floated" — she floated, she did not swim across.

ra_g2_03.title: Leo's Kite
ra_g2_03.text: Leo made a kite out of paper and sticks. He ran across the field, but the kite just bumped along the grass. Grandpa watched and said, "Try a longer tail." Leo tied on a long strip of cloth. This time the kite rose up and up until it looked as small as a bird.

q.text: "The kite rose up and up." What does rose mean here?
q.why: "Rose up and up until it looked as small as a bird" — it went higher and higher.

q.text: What did Leo tie on for a tail?
q.why: "Leo tied on a long strip of cloth."

q.text: Why did Grandpa tell Leo to try a longer tail?
c: to make the kite heavy so it falls
q.why: Before the tail the kite "bumped along the grass"; after it, "the kite rose up."

ra_g2_04.title: Slow and Sleepy Sloths
ra_g2_04.text: Sloths live high in the trees of warm rain forests. They move very slowly and sleep for much of the day. A sloth hangs upside down by its long, curved claws and eats leaves. Tiny green plants called algae can grow in its fur. The algae help the sloth blend in with the leaves.

q.text: How does a sloth hang in a tree?
q.why: "A sloth hangs upside down by its long, curved claws."

q.text: In this passage, what are algae?
q.why: "Tiny green plants called algae can grow in its fur."

q.text: What is this mostly about?
c: why it rains in rain forests
q.why: Every sentence tells something about sloths: where they live, how they move, what they eat.

ra_g2_05.title: Grow a Bean Plant
ra_g2_05.text: Here is how to grow a bean plant. First, fill a cup with soil. Next, push a bean seed into the soil, about as deep as your finger to the first bend. Then give it a little water and put the cup in a sunny window. Keep the soil damp, but not soggy. In a week or so, a green sprout will poke up.

q.text: What do you do first?
c: put the cup in a window
q.why: "First, fill a cup with soil."

q.text: "Keep the soil damp, but not soggy." What does damp mean?
q.why: Damp is less wet than soggy — just a little wet.

q.text: What do these steps help you do?
c: make a cup of soil to sell
q.why: The first sentence says it: "Here is how to grow a bean plant."

ra_g2_06.title: Hummingbirds
ra_g2_06.text: Hummingbirds are some of the smallest birds in the world. Their wings beat so fast that they make a humming sound. That is how the birds got their name. A hummingbird can hover in one spot. It can even fly backward! It sips sweet nectar from flowers with its long, thin beak.

q.text: How did hummingbirds get their name?
c: from the sound of their wings
q.why: "Their wings beat so fast that they make a humming sound. That is how the birds got their name."

q.text: "A hummingbird can hover in one spot." What does hover mean?
q.why: "Hover in one spot" — it stays in one place while flying.

q.text: What is this mostly about?
q.why: Every sentence tells something special about hummingbirds.

ra_g2_07.title: How a Rainbow Is Made
ra_g2_07.text: Sometimes the sun shines while it rains. That is a good time to look for a rainbow. Sunlight looks white. But it is really made of many colors. When the sun shines through raindrops, the colors spread out. To find a rainbow, stand with the sun behind you. The rain should be in front of you.

q.text: What is sunlight really made of?
q.why: "Sunlight looks white. But it is really made of many colors."

q.text: Where should the sun be when you look for a rainbow?
q.why: "Stand with the sun behind you. The rain should be in front of you."

q.text: What is the best title?
q.why: The passage tells what makes a rainbow and how to find one.

ra_g2_08.title: Penguin Dads
ra_g2_08.text: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Their wings work like flippers, so they are fast swimmers. Emperor penguins live in icy Antarctica. The mother lays one egg. The father holds it on his feet under a warm fold of skin. He keeps it safe for about two months. The mother goes to find food in the sea.

q.text: What do a penguin's wings work like?
q.why: "Their wings work like flippers."

q.text: Who keeps the emperor penguin egg warm?
q.why: "The father holds it on his feet under a warm fold of skin."

q.text: Why does the father keep the egg under a fold of skin?
c: to hide it from the mother
to keep it warm on the ice
q.why: They live in "icy Antarctica," and the fold of skin is "warm."

ra_g2_09.title: The Missing Library Book
ra_g2_09.text: Ava could not find her library book. It was due today! She looked under her bed. She looked in her backpack. Then she remembered reading it in the car. She ran outside. There it was, stuck between the seats! Ava made a new rule: library books stay on one shelf from now on.

q.text: Where was the book?
q.why: "There it was, stuck between the seats!" She looked under the bed and in the backpack first.

q.text: The book was due today. What does due mean?
c: it had to go back today
q.why: She was rushing to find it because it was due — it had to be returned that day.

q.text: Why did Ava make a new rule?
c: so she won't lose one again
q.why: Right after she found the lost book, she said books "stay on one shelf from now on."

ra_g2_10.title: The Lemonade Stand
ra_g2_10.text: On a hot day, Rosa and her brother set up a lemonade stand. Nobody stopped. Rosa looked around and saw why. Their table was in the shade behind a big bush. No one could see it! They moved the table out to the sidewalk. Then they made a big, bright sign. Soon a line of thirsty people was waiting.

q.text: Where was the table at first?
q.why: "Their table was in the shade behind a big bush." They moved it to the sidewalk later.

q.text: Why did nobody stop at first?
c: No one could see the stand.
q.why: "No one could see it!" Once they moved it and made a sign, people came.

q.text: The people were thirsty. What does thirsty mean?
q.why: It was a hot day and they lined up for lemonade — they wanted a drink.

ra_g2_11.title: The Plant That Eats Bugs
ra_g2_11.text: The Venus flytrap is a plant that eats bugs. It grows wild in only one small part of the world, near the coast of North and South Carolina. Each leaf opens like a little mouth. When a bug walks in and bumps the tiny hairs inside, snap! The leaf shuts tight. Then the plant slowly turns the bug into food.

q.text: Where does the Venus flytrap grow wild?
q.why: "It grows wild in only one small part of the world, near the coast of North and South Carolina."

q.text: What makes the leaf shut?
c: a bug bumping the tiny hairs
q.why: "When a bug walks in and bumps the tiny hairs inside, snap! The leaf shuts tight."

q.text: What is this mostly about?
c: plants that grow in the sea
q.why: It tells what the flytrap is, where it grows, and how it catches and eats bugs.

ra_g2_12.title: The Tallest Mountain in the East
ra_g2_12.text: Mount Mitchell is in the mountains of North Carolina. It is the tallest mountain in the East. At the top, it can be cold and windy, even in summer. Thick fog often hides the view. But on a clear day, you can see for miles and miles.

q.text: Where is Mount Mitchell?
q.why: "Mount Mitchell is in the mountains of North Carolina."

q.text: What should you bring to the top in summer?
q.why: "At the top, it can be cold and windy, even in summer."

q.text: "On a clear day" — what is a clear day?
c: a day with lots of rain
a day with no fog or clouds
q.why: On a clear day the fog is gone, so "you can see for miles and miles."

ra_g2_13.title: The Lighthouse That Moved
ra_g2_13.text: The lighthouse at Cape Hatteras is very tall. It stands by the sea in North Carolina. Black and white stripes twist around it like a candy cane. Year by year, the sea crept closer to it. So in 1999, workers moved the whole lighthouse back from the water. It took weeks, but it got there safe and sound.

q.text: Why did workers move the lighthouse?
c: The sea was getting too close.
q.why: "Year by year, the sea crept closer to it. So in 1999, workers moved the whole lighthouse."

q.text: What do the stripes look like?
q.why: "Black and white stripes twist around it like a candy cane."

q.text: Was the lighthouse moved quickly?
q.why: "It took weeks, but it got there safe and sound."

ra_g2_14.title: Sweet Potato State
ra_g2_14.text: North Carolina grows more sweet potatoes than any other state. They grow under the ground, like carrots do. Farmers dig them up in the fall. The insides are orange. They taste sweet when you bake them. Some people even make them into pie!

q.text: Where do sweet potatoes grow?
q.why: "They grow under the ground, like carrots do."

q.text: When do farmers dig them up?
q.why: "Farmers dig them up in the fall."

q.text: What is this mostly about?
q.why: Every sentence tells something about sweet potatoes.

ra_g2_15.title: No Blinking
ra_g2_15.text: Have you ever seen a snake blink? You never will! Snakes do not have eyelids. Instead, each eye is covered by a clear scale, like a tiny window. That is why a snake always seems to be staring at you. When a snake sheds its skin, the clear scales come off too.

q.text: Why can't a snake blink?
q.why: "Snakes do not have eyelids."

q.text: What covers a snake's eye?
c: a bit of skin that opens
q.why: "Each eye is covered by a clear scale, like a tiny window."

q.text: Why does a snake always seem to be staring?
q.why: No eyelids means its eyes are always open — "That is why a snake always seems to be staring."

ra_g2_16.title: A Snake That Helps Farmers
ra_g2_16.text: In most of North Carolina, the rat snake is a long black snake. It has no venom, the poison some snakes have in their bite. It eats mice and rats, so farmers are often glad to have one near the barn. Rat snakes are good climbers, too. They can slither right up a tree!

q.text: Why are farmers glad to have a rat snake near the barn?
q.why: "It eats mice and rats, so farmers are often glad to have one near the barn."

q.text: What is venom?
q.why: The passage tells you: "venom, the poison some snakes have in their bite."

q.text: Where can a rat snake climb?
q.why: "They can slither right up a tree!"

ra_g2_17.title: How Snakes Move
ra_g2_17.text: A snake has no legs, but it can still move fast. It pushes its body against the ground, rocks, and sticks. Wide scales on its belly grip the ground like the bottom of a sneaker. Its body bends side to side in an S shape. Some snakes can even swim this way!

q.text: What helps a snake grip the ground?
q.why: "Wide scales on its belly grip the ground like the bottom of a sneaker."

q.text: What shape does its body make?
q.why: "Its body bends side to side in an S shape."

q.text: What is this mostly about?
c: how to swim fast in a lake
q.why: Every sentence tells how a snake moves without legs.

ra_g2_18.title: Dinosaur Cousins
ra_g2_18.text: Here is a big surprise. Birds come from dinosaurs! Some fossils show that some of them had feathers. Long, long ago, some small ones slowly changed into the first birds. So a robin in your yard is a distant cousin of the dinosaurs. A distant cousin is part of your family, but not close.

q.text: What do some fossils show?
q.why: "Some fossils show that some of them had feathers."

q.text: In this passage, what is a distant cousin?
c: a cousin you see a lot
a cousin who is very old
q.why: The passage says it: "A distant cousin is part of your family, but not close."

q.text: What is the big idea?
q.why: "Here is a big surprise. Birds come from dinosaurs!" The rest explains it.

ra_g2_19.title: Tiny Arms, Big Teeth
ra_g2_19.text: Tyrannosaurus rex was a giant dinosaur. It ate meat. It had huge jaws, and some of its teeth were as long as a banana! But its arms were short. They looked small next to its big body. Scientists still are not sure what its small arms were for.

q.text: How long were some of its teeth?
q.why: "Some of its teeth were as long as a banana!"

q.text: What did it eat?
q.why: "It ate meat."

q.text: Do scientists know for sure what its arms were for?
c: No, they are still not sure.
q.why: "Scientists still are not sure what its small arms were for."

ra_g2_20.title: Three Horns
ra_g2_20.text: Triceratops was a big dinosaur. It had three horns on its face. Two long horns grew above its eyes. A short one grew on its nose. A wide, bony frill fanned out behind its head like a big collar. It had all those horns, but it ate only plants.

q.text: Where was the short horn?
q.why: "Two long horns grew above its eyes. A short one grew on its nose."

q.text: What was the frill?
c: a bony fan behind its head
q.why: "A wide, bony frill fanned out behind its head like a big collar."

q.text: What did Triceratops eat?
q.why: "It had all those horns, but it ate only plants."

ra_g2_21.title: Spring Peepers
ra_g2_21.text: On early spring nights, you may hear "peep, peep, peep" from the woods. It sounds like birds, but it is really tiny frogs called spring peepers. Each one is only about as long as a paper clip. The males peep to call the females. A pond full of peepers can be very loud!

q.text: What makes the peeping sound?
q.why: "It sounds like birds, but it is really tiny frogs called spring peepers."

q.text: How big is a spring peeper?
c: about as long as a paper clip
about as long as a pencil
about as big as a cat
q.why: "Each one is only about as long as a paper clip."

q.text: Why do the males peep?
q.why: "The males peep to call the females."

ra_g2_22.title: Frog or Toad?
ra_g2_22.text: Frogs and toads look a lot alike, but you can tell them apart. Most frogs have smooth, wet skin and long legs for big leaps. Most toads have dry, bumpy skin and short legs for small hops. Frogs like to stay near water. Toads can live in dry gardens.

q.text: Which one has dry, bumpy skin?
q.why: "Most toads have dry, bumpy skin and short legs."

q.text: An animal with long legs takes a big leap into a pond. What is it most likely?
q.why: Frogs have "long legs for big leaps" and "like to stay near water."

q.text: What is this mostly about?
c: how to catch a toad in a garden
how frogs and toads are different
why frogs like to swim in rain
q.why: "You can tell them apart" — the rest lists the differences.

ra_g2_23.title: The Puppy Who Would Not Come
ra_g2_23.text: Omar's new puppy ran across the yard. "Come here!" Omar called, and he ran after her. The puppy ran even faster. Then Omar had an idea. He sat down on the grass and called her name softly. The puppy stopped, turned around, and trotted right into his lap.

q.text: What did Omar do first?
q.why: "'Come here!' Omar called, and he ran after her." Sitting down came later.

q.text: Why did the puppy come at the end?
q.why: When Omar chased, she ran faster. When he sat and called softly, she came.

q.text: What does Omar learn?
c: Chasing a puppy makes it run.
Grass is soft to sit on.
q.why: Running after her made her run "even faster"; sitting still worked.

ra_g2_24.title: Taking Turns
ra_g2_24.text: There was one swing and two kids. Lena wanted it, and so did Kai. They both pulled on the chain. Then Lena said, "Let's take turns. You swing while I count to fifty, and then it's my turn." Kai liked that plan. They swung all afternoon without one fight.

q.text: What did both kids want?
q.why: "There was one swing and two kids. Lena wanted it, and so did Kai."

q.text: How long was each turn?
c: for one minute on a clock
q.why: "You swing while I count to fifty, and then it's my turn."

q.text: Did the plan work?
q.why: "They swung all afternoon without one fight."

ra_g2_25.title: The Ball in the Tree
ra_g2_25.text: Gus kicked his yellow ball so high that it got stuck at the very top of a maple tree. He jumped and jumped, but he could not reach it. He threw a stick at it, but the ball did not move at all. Then he asked his neighbor, Mr. Bell, for help. Mr. Bell got a tall ladder, and the ball was back in a minute.

q.text: What did Gus try first?
q.why: "He jumped and jumped, but he could not reach it." The stick came next, then Mr. Bell.

q.text: Why did Gus ask Mr. Bell for help?
c: He could not get the ball down himself.
He wanted to borrow a stick.
q.why: He jumped and threw a stick, and neither worked.

q.text: How did the ball come down?
q.why: "Mr. Bell got a tall ladder, and the ball was back in a minute."

ra_g2_26.title: Where Did Nibbles Go?
ra_g2_26.text: Nibbles the hamster got out of her cage. The class looked everywhere, but she was gone. Then Ms. Park had an idea. She put a few seeds in each corner of the room. In the morning, the seeds by the bookshelf were gone. There was Nibbles, asleep behind the books!

q.text: Why did Ms. Park put out seeds?
c: to find out where Nibbles was
to plant a garden in class
q.why: The missing seeds showed where Nibbles had been — "the seeds by the bookshelf were gone."

q.text: Where was Nibbles?
q.why: "There was Nibbles, asleep behind the books!"

q.text: What is the best title?
q.why: Ms. Park's seed trick is how the class finds Nibbles.

ra_g2_27.title: The Spilled Paint
ra_g2_27.text: Nina was painting a picture of the sea. Oops! Her elbow bumped the cup, and a big blob of blue paint spilled across the page. She almost cried. Then she looked again. The blob looked like a whale! She gave it a tail, an eye, and a spray of water.

q.text: How did Nina feel when the paint spilled?
q.why: "She almost cried."

q.text: What did the blob look like?
q.why: "The blob looked like a whale!"

q.text: What does the story show?
c: Paint is very hard to clean up.
A mistake can turn into something good.
Whales like to live in the sea.
q.why: The spill became a whale in her picture.

ra_g2_28.title: Snow Day
ra_g2_28.text:
Snow on the rooftop.
Snow on the hill.
Snow on the mailbox
And the windowsill.
Mittens and boots on,
Out the door we go
To build a big snow fort
And slide down the snow!
Back home for cocoa,
Our cheeks rosy red,
And wet mittens drying
By the fire before bed.

q.text: Where is the snow in the poem?
q.why: "Snow on the rooftop. / Snow on the hill."

q.text: What do they put on?
q.why: "Mittens and boots on, / Out the door we go."

q.text: How do the kids feel about the snow?
q.why: They rush "out the door" to build a fort and slide — they can't wait.

ra_g2_29.title: A Letter About Snow
ra_g2_29.text:
Dear Sofia,
It snowed here last night! The whole yard is white, and the pond froze. My brother and I built a snow fort with a door and a window. Does it ever snow where you live? Please write back and tell me.
Your friend,
June

q.text: What did June and her brother build?
q.why: "My brother and I built a snow fort with a door and a window."

q.text: Why does June ask if it snows where Sofia lives?
q.why: She asks "Does it ever snow where you live?" and wants Sofia to "write back and tell me."

q.text: Why did June write this letter?
c: to say she is sick in bed
to ask Sofia for a new sled
to tell about the snow and ask a question
q.why: She tells what the snow was like, then asks Sofia about her home.

ra_g2_30.title: Orange Bird Feeder
ra_g2_30.text: You can make a bird feeder out of an orange. First, ask a grown-up to cut an orange in half. Scoop out the fruit and eat it! Next, poke two holes near the top edge and tie a string through them. Fill the orange cup with birdseed. Then hang it on a branch and watch the birds come.

q.text: What is the first step?
c: Ask a grown-up to cut it.
Hang it on a high branch.
q.why: "First, ask a grown-up to cut an orange in half."

q.text: Why do you poke two holes?
c: so a string can go through
q.why: "Poke two holes near the top edge and tie a string through them."

q.text: What do these steps help you make?
q.why: "You can make a bird feeder out of an orange."

ra_g2_31.title: Harriet Tubman Goes Back
ra_g2_31.text: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland. In 1849, she ran away to the North, where she was free. But she did not stay safe there. She went back again and again to lead others out. She led about seventy people in all. She walked at night and followed the North Star. Harriet had strong faith. She prayed as she went. She said God showed her the way.

q.text: What did Harriet do after she was free?
c: She stayed safe in the North.
She sailed far out to sea.
She went back to lead others out.
q.why: "She went back again and again to lead others out. She led about seventy people in all."

q.text: When did she walk?
q.why: "She walked at night and followed the North Star."

q.text: What helped Harriet be so brave?
q.why: "Harriet had strong faith. She prayed as she went. She said God showed her the way."

ra_g3_01.title: The Squeaky Gate
ra_g3_01.text: Every morning, the gate in Nora's yard let out a loud squeak. It woke the baby, and it made the dog bark. Nora asked her mom what to do. "Gates squeak when metal parts rub together," Mom said. "A drop of oil helps them slide." Nora found a small can of oil in the garage. She put a few drops on each hinge, the metal joint that lets the gate swing. Then she swung the gate back and forth. Not a sound! The next morning, the baby slept late, and so did the dog.

q.text: What is a hinge?
c: the metal joint that lets a gate swing
the top board of a fence
q.why: The story tells you: "each hinge, the metal joint that lets the gate swing."

q.text: What makes a gate squeak, according to Mom?
q.why: Mom says, "Gates squeak when metal parts rub together."

q.text: Why did the baby sleep late the next morning?
c: The gate did not squeak anymore.
q.why: The squeak used to wake the baby. After the oil there was "Not a sound!"

q.text: What is the best title for this story?
q.why: The story is about Nora solving the squeak. The baby and dog are only part of it.

ra_g3_02.title: The Tallest Tower
ra_g3_02.text: Marcus wanted to build the tallest block tower he had ever made. He stacked the blocks straight up, one on top of another. At ten blocks high, the tower wobbled and crashed. His friend Dee had an idea. "Look at real towers," she said. "They are wide at the bottom." Marcus started over. This time he made a wide base of eight blocks. Every few layers, he used one fewer block as he went up. His new tower was steady, and it stood fifteen blocks tall.

q.text: What happened to the first tower?
q.why: "At ten blocks high, the tower wobbled and crashed." Fifteen was the second tower.

q.text: "He made a wide base of eight blocks." What is a base?
q.why: Dee said towers "are wide at the bottom," and the base is where Marcus made it wide.

q.text: Why did the second tower stay up?
c: It was wide at the bottom.
It was shorter than the first.
q.why: Dee's idea was a wide bottom, and "his new tower was steady." It was taller, not shorter.

q.text: What lesson does Marcus learn?
c: It is better to build alone.
A wide bottom makes a tower steady.
q.why: He followed Dee's "wide at the bottom" idea and the tower held.

ra_g3_03.title: Fireflies
ra_g3_03.text:
When the summer sun goes down
And the sky is dark and deep,
Tiny lights blink on and off.
All the robins are asleep.

Each one flashes out a signal.
Short and long, it sends a code,
Calling to another firefly
Down the dark and quiet road.

Some are high above the bushes.
Some are low beside my knee.
Blink and wait, and blink again.
Are they flashing back at me?

I could catch them in a jar,
But I watch and let them glow.
They belong out in the night,
So I sit and watch the show.

q.text: When do the fireflies come out in the poem?
q.why: "When the summer sun goes down / ... Tiny lights blink on and off."

q.text: "Each one flashes out a signal." What is a signal?
q.why: Each flash "sends a code, / Calling to another firefly" — a message without words.

q.text: Why doesn't the poet catch the fireflies?
c: The poet thinks they belong outside.
q.why: "I could catch them in a jar, / But ... They belong out in the night."

q.text: What is the poem mostly about?
c: watching fireflies on a summer night
q.why: The whole poem describes the fireflies' lights and the poet watching them.

ra_g3_04.title: Lost Cat
ra_g3_04.text:
LOST CAT
Have you seen Pepper? She is a small gray cat with one white paw and a green collar. She slipped out our back door on Saturday evening. Pepper is very shy, so she may hide under porches or in sheds. Please do not chase her, or she will run farther away. She will come if you call her name softly and shake a bag of treats. If you see her, please leave a note at the yellow house on Elm Street. We miss her very much. Thank you for looking!

q.text: What color is Pepper's collar?
q.why: "A small gray cat with one white paw and a green collar." Yellow is the house.

q.text: Where would be a good place to look for Pepper?
c: at the top of a tall tree
q.why: "She may hide under porches or in sheds."

q.text: "She slipped out our back door." What does slipped out mean here?
q.why: Nobody meant to let her go — she got out by accident, and that is why she is lost. It was the back door, not the front.

q.text: Why was this notice written?
c: to get help finding a lost cat
to tell people about Elm Street
to give away a green collar
q.why: The title is LOST CAT and it asks, "Have you seen Pepper?"

ra_g3_05.title: Spiders Are Not Insects
ra_g3_05.text: Many people call spiders bugs, but spiders are not insects. An insect has six legs and three body parts. A spider has eight legs and only two body parts. All spiders can make silk inside their bodies. Many use it to weave webs that trap flies. Others, like the jumping spider, do not catch food in webs at all. They sneak up on their prey and pounce. Spiders help people, too. They eat many insects that bother us or nibble garden plants.

q.text: How many legs does a spider have?
q.why: "A spider has eight legs." Six legs is an insect.

q.text: "They sneak up on their prey." What is prey?
c: an animal that is hunted for food
q.why: Jumping spiders sneak up and pounce on their prey — the animal they are catching to eat.

q.text: Why might a gardener be glad to see a spider?
c: Spiders eat insects that nibble plants.
q.why: "They eat many insects that bother us or nibble garden plants."

q.text: What is the main idea?
c: Spiders are different from insects, and they help us.
Jumping spiders are the biggest spiders.
q.why: The passage shows how spiders differ from insects, then tells how they help. Not all spiders use webs.

ra_g3_06.title: Make a Cup Telephone
ra_g3_06.text: You can talk to a friend with two paper cups and a long string. First, ask a grown-up to poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup. Push one end of the string through each hole. Tie a big knot inside each cup so the string cannot slip out. Now you and your friend each take a cup and walk apart until the string is tight. One person talks into a cup. The other holds a cup to one ear. Your voice makes the string vibrate, or shake very fast, and the shaking carries the sound.

q.text: What should you do right after you push the string through the holes?
c: Tie a big knot inside each cup.
q.why: "Push one end of the string through each hole. Tie a big knot inside each cup."

q.text: What does vibrate mean in these steps?
q.why: The steps tell you: "vibrate, or shake very fast."

q.text: What would happen if you forgot to tie the knots?
c: The string could slip out of the cups.
Your friend would have to whisper.
q.why: The knot is there "so the string cannot slip out."

q.text: What is the best title for these steps?
c: Sending Your Voice Down a String
How to Fix a Paper Cup
q.why: The steps show how a string between two cups carries your voice.

ra_g3_07.title: The Garden Mystery
ra_g3_07.text: Something was eating Grandma's lettuce. Every morning, more leaves were nibbled down to tiny stubs. Jada decided to be a detective. She looked for clues in the garden. In the soft dirt she found small paw prints. On a twig by the fence, she found a tuft of fluffy brown fur. "A rabbit!" she told Grandma. Together they put up a short wire fence around the lettuce. They pushed the bottom of it into the ground so the rabbit could not dig under. The next morning, every leaf was safe.

q.text: What was being eaten?
q.why: The first sentence: "Something was eating Grandma's lettuce."

q.text: "She looked for clues in the garden." What are clues?
c: things that help you figure something out
q.why: Jada was being a detective; the paw prints and fur helped her figure out the answer.

q.text: How did Jada figure out it was a rabbit?
c: She found paw prints and fluffy fur.
She heard it in the night.
q.why: She found "small paw prints" and "a tuft of fluffy brown fur," then said "A rabbit!"

q.text: Why did they push the bottom of the fence into the ground?
c: so the fence would look nice
so the rabbit could not dig under
q.why: "So the rabbit could not dig under."

ra_g3_08.title: Why Leaves Change Color
ra_g3_08.text: In summer, most leaves are green. They are green because of chlorophyll, which helps the tree make food from sunlight. But leaves also hold yellow and orange colors. In summer, the green covers them up. When fall comes, the days get shorter and cooler. The tree stops making chlorophyll, and the green slowly fades. Then the yellow and orange that were hiding all along can finally show. Some trees, like many maples, also make bright red colors in the fall. After a few weeks, the leaves dry up and drop to the ground.

q.text: What makes leaves green?
q.why: "They are green because of chlorophyll."

q.text: Were the yellow colors in the leaves during the summer?
c: No, they grow in the fall.
Only on trees that turn red.
Yes, but the green covered them.
q.why: "The yellow and orange that were hiding all along" — they were there, covered by green.

q.text: "The green slowly fades." What does fades mean?
q.why: When the tree stops making chlorophyll, the green goes away so the other colors can show.

q.text: What is this passage mostly about?
c: why leaves change color in fall
q.why: The title and every sentence explain the color change in fall.

ra_g3_09.title: Twelve Seconds in the Air
ra_g3_09.text: Wilbur and Orville Wright were brothers. They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. They loved to study how birds fly. For years they built gliders and tested them. A glider has no engine. On December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, they tried a new airplane that had one. Orville lay on the wing as the engine roared. The plane rose into the air and flew for about twelve seconds. It was the first powered airplane flight that a pilot could control. It was short, but it changed the world.

q.text: How long did that first flight last?
q.why: "The plane ... flew for about twelve seconds."

q.text: What kind of shop did the Wright brothers run?
q.why: "They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio."

q.text: "The first powered airplane flight" — what does powered mean here?
q.why: "A glider has no engine." The new airplane "had one" — that is what made the flight powered.

q.text: Why did the brothers study birds?
c: to sell them in their shop
to learn how things can fly
q.why: "They loved to study how birds fly" while they worked on flying machines.

ra_g3_10.title: The Camel's Hump
ra_g3_10.text: Most camels live in hot, dry deserts. Many people think a camel's hump is full of water, but it is not. The hump stores fat. When food is hard to find, the camel's body can use that fat for energy. Camels can go many days without drinking. When they find water, they can drink a lot very quickly. Long eyelashes help keep blowing sand out of their eyes. They can also close their nostrils to keep sand out of their noses. Wide, padded feet keep them from sinking in soft sand. For thousands of years, people have used camels to carry heavy loads across the desert.

q.text: What does a camel's hump store?
q.why: "The hump stores fat." The passage says it is NOT full of water.

q.text: What mistake do many people make about camels?
c: They think camels live in snow.
They think camels have short eyelashes.
They think the hump holds water.
q.why: "Many people think a camel's hump is full of water, but it is not."

q.text: "Wide, padded feet" — what does padded mean?
q.why: Padded feet are cushioned — soft and thick — and wide, so they don't sink.

q.text: What is the main idea?
c: Camels drink only once a year.
A camel's body is built for the desert.
Sand can get in your eyes.
q.why: Hump, eyelashes and feet are all ways a camel is ready for desert life.

ra_g3_11.title: The Lady with the Lamp
ra_g3_11.text: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820. Her English family was rich. In those days, girls like her were not supposed to have jobs. But when she was sixteen, Florence felt that God was calling her to help others. Years later, she chose to become a nurse. At first, her parents did not want her to. In 1854, during a war, she took a team of nurses to an army hospital. It was dirty and crowded. Many soldiers were sick. Florence had it scrubbed clean. She got them clean clothes and better food. At night she walked the wards, the long hospital rooms, with a lamp in her hand. She became known as "the Lady with the Lamp."

q.text: What did Florence feel when she was sixteen?
c: that she wanted to grow up to be a soldier
that God was calling her to help others
that she should stay home with her family
q.why: "When she was sixteen, Florence felt that God was calling her to help others."

q.text: "She walked the wards." What are wards?
q.why: The passage tells you: "the wards, the long hospital rooms."

q.text: Why was she called "the Lady with the Lamp"?
c: She checked on them at night carrying a lamp.
She lit the hospital's lamps each morning.
q.why: "At night she walked the wards ... with a lamp in her hand."

q.text: What is this passage mostly about?
c: how Florence's calling led her to nursing
how the nurses kept an army hospital clean
the rich family Florence grew up in
why the soldiers went off to war
q.why: It follows Florence from her calling at sixteen to her work in the army hospital.

ra_g4_01.title: Thin Ice
ra_g4_01.text: After three cold nights, the pond behind the school was covered with a thin sheet of white ice. "Let's slide across!" said Simon, stepping toward the edge. Hana grabbed his sleeve. "My aunt says ice has to be really thick before it is safe to walk on," she said. "It only got cold a few days ago." Simon rolled his eyes, but he stepped back. Hana picked up a heavy rock and tossed it a few feet out onto the ice. With a sharp crack, the rock broke right through, and dark water splashed up around it. The two friends stared at the hole without a word. Finally Simon spoke. "Maybe we could go sledding instead," he said quietly. Hana laughed, and they ran off to find a hill.

q.text: "A thin sheet of white ice." What is a sheet here?
q.why: The ice lay across the pond in a thin, flat layer.

q.text: Why did Hana throw the rock?
c: to test whether the ice was strong
to break the ice for the fish
to see how far she could throw
q.why: She had just said ice must be thick to be safe; the rock showed it was not.

q.text: Why does Simon speak "quietly" at the end?
c: He is too cold to talk.
He is scared by what almost happened.
q.why: He had wanted to slide; then he saw the rock break "right through." He changes his plan to sledding.

q.text: Why did Hana think the ice was not safe yet?
c: It had only been cold for a few days.
She saw a crack in it.
q.why: "It only got cold a few days ago."

ra_g4_02.title: Seeing with Sound
ra_g4_02.text: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Many bats hunt insects at night, when it is too dark to see well. So how do they find their food? They use their ears. As a bat flies, it makes high squeaks, and most of them are too high for people to hear. The sound bounces off moths, trees, and walls and comes back as an echo. By listening to the echoes, the bat can tell where things are and how big they are. This is called echolocation. With it, a bat can snatch a tiny insect out of the air in complete darkness. Bats are not the only animals that do this. Dolphins and some whales use echolocation too, sending clicks through the water.

q.text: What does a bat listen to so it can find food?
c: the echoes of its own squeaks
q.why: "By listening to the echoes, the bat can tell where things are."

q.text: What is echolocation?
c: finding things by listening to echoes
q.why: The passage explains echoes, then says "This is called echolocation."

q.text: Why is echolocation so useful to bats?
c: It lets them hunt when it is too dark to see.
It helps them sleep upside down.
q.why: They hunt "at night, when it is too dark to see well," and echolocation works "in complete darkness."

q.text: What is the main idea?
c: Bats find food in the dark by using sound.
q.why: Most of the passage explains how bats use echoes to hunt. The other choices are small details.

ra_g4_03.title: The Bake Sale Mix-Up
ra_g4_03.text: The night before the bake sale, Priya and her dad baked four dozen cookies. In the morning, Priya bit into one to make sure they were perfect. Her face scrunched up. The cookie was terribly salty! She looked at the two plain white jars on the counter. Neither jar had a label. Late last night, they must have scooped salt instead of sugar. There was no time to bake again, so Priya came up with a new plan. She and her dad made a big jug of lemonade, and she taped a sign to the table: "Fresh Lemonade — Cookies Next Week!" The lemonade was gone by noon. That evening, Priya found a marker. In big letters, she wrote SALT on one jar and SUGAR on the other.

q.text: How did Priya find out something was wrong?
q.why: "Priya bit into one to make sure they were perfect ... The cookie was terribly salty!"

q.text: Why did they use salt by mistake?
c: The recipe said to use salt.
The two jars looked the same and had no labels.
q.why: "Two plain white jars ... Neither jar had a label."

q.text: "Her face scrunched up." What does that show?
c: She was laughing at a joke.
She made a face because the taste was bad.
q.why: Right after her face scrunched up we learn "The cookie was terribly salty!"

q.text: What is the best title for this story?
q.why: The cookies failed, but Priya's lemonade plan sold out — she saved the sale. The lemonade was not salty.

ra_g4_04.title: Nature's Builders
ra_g4_04.text: Beavers are nature's builders. With their strong front teeth, they chew through tree trunks and drag the branches to a stream. They pile up sticks, stones, and mud to make a dam. The dam holds back the water and makes a quiet pond. In the pond, beavers build a home called a lodge. Its doors are underwater, which helps keep out animals like wolves and coyotes. When the dam springs a leak, the beavers quickly patch it with more mud and sticks. A beaver's front teeth never stop growing, so all that chewing keeps them from getting too long. The teeth are orange because they contain iron, which makes them extra strong. Beaver ponds help other animals, too. Frogs, ducks, fish, and even moose may come to live near the water.

q.text: What do beavers use to build a dam?
q.why: "They pile up sticks, stones, and mud to make a dam."

q.text: What is a lodge in this passage?
c: a beaver's home in the pond
q.why: "In the pond, beavers build a home called a lodge."

q.text: What would probably happen to a beaver that stopped chewing?
c: Its teeth would grow too long.
It would build a bigger dam.
Wolves would get into its lodge.
q.why: The teeth "never stop growing, so all that chewing keeps them from getting too long."

q.text: What is the main idea?
c: Beavers build dams and homes that change the land and help other animals.
Beaver teeth are orange because they have iron in them.
Wolves and coyotes try to get into beaver lodges.
Moose, ducks, and frogs like to live near ponds.
q.why: The passage tells what beavers build and how their ponds help others. The rest are details.

ra_g4_05.title: A Map for Lina
ra_g4_05.text: A new family moved into the blue house across the street. Their daughter, Lina, did not know her way around yet, so Ruby decided to help. She spread out a large sheet of paper and drew their street right in the middle. She added the park at the north end, the library around the corner, and the ice cream shop two blocks east. In one corner she drew a compass rose with N, S, E, and W. Then she made a key: a small tree meant a park, a book meant the library, and a cone meant ice cream. Ruby rolled the map up, tied it with a ribbon, and carried it across the street. Lina studied it for a long time. "Can we start with the cone?" she asked with a grin.

q.text: On Ruby's map, what is the key?
c: a list that tells what the little pictures mean
q.why: "She made a key: a small tree meant a park, a book meant the library, and a cone meant ice cream."

q.text: Where does Lina want to go first?
q.why: On the key, "a cone meant ice cream," and Lina asks to "start with the cone."

q.text: What did Ruby draw in one corner of the map?
q.why: "In one corner she drew a compass rose with N, S, E, and W."

q.text: Why did Ruby make the map?
c: to find a lost library book
to show where she buried a treasure
to help Lina learn her way around
q.why: "Lina did not know her way around yet, so Ruby decided to help."

ra_g4_06.title: Make Walking Water
ra_g4_06.text: Can water walk? With this trick, it seems to! You will need three clear cups, two paper towels, water, and red and blue food coloring. First, line up the three cups in a row. Fill the two outside cups with water and leave the middle cup empty. Add red coloring to one full cup and blue to the other. Next, fold each paper towel the long way into a thin strip. Bend one strip so that one end sits in the red water and the other end hangs into the empty cup. Do the same with the blue cup. Now wait and watch. The water slowly climbs up the paper and drips into the middle cup. This works because paper towels are full of tiny spaces that soak up, or absorb, water. In a few hours, the middle cup fills partway with purple water!

q.text: Which cup do you leave empty at the start?
q.why: "Fill the two outside cups with water and leave the middle cup empty."

q.text: What does absorb mean in these steps?
q.why: The steps tell you: "soak up, or absorb, water."

q.text: Why does the water in the middle cup turn purple?
c: The paper towels turn the water purple.
Red and blue water both drip in and mix.
The water sits in the sun.
You add purple coloring at the end.
q.why: Red walks in from one side and blue from the other; red and blue mixed make purple.

q.text: What do you do right after you fill the two outside cups?
c: Fold each paper towel into a thin strip.
Wait and watch the water climb.
Add red coloring to one and blue to the other.
Line up the three cups in a row.
q.why: "Fill the two outside cups ... Add red coloring to one full cup and blue to the other."

ra_g4_07.title: Dots That Speak
ra_g4_07.text: Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. When he was three, he hurt his eye while playing in his father's workshop. An infection spread, and by age five he was blind in both eyes. Louis was a bright student, and he went to a school for blind children in Paris. The school had a few books with large raised letters, but they were huge and slow to read by touch. When he was about fifteen, Louis invented a better way. He used patterns of raised dots, with up to six dots in each small cell. Each pattern stood for a letter. Fingers could feel the dots quickly. Today, people all over the world read braille, and you may see it on elevator buttons and signs.

q.text: How many dots can be in one braille cell?
q.why: "Patterns of raised dots, with up to six dots in each small cell."

q.text: In this passage, what is a cell?
c: a tiny part of a living thing
a small space that holds one dot pattern
q.why: "Up to six dots in each small cell. Each pattern stood for a letter."

q.text: Why was Louis's idea better than the raised-letter books?
c: Fingers could read the dots quickly.
It was printed in bright colors.
It did not need to be touched.
q.why: The old books were "huge and slow to read by touch"; with braille, "fingers could feel the dots quickly."

q.text: What is the best title?
c: The Boy Who Gave Books to Fingers
q.why: The passage is about how young Louis Braille invented a way to read by touch.

ra_g4_08.title: The Same Old Water
ra_g4_08.text: The water you drink is not new. Earth has used the same water over and over for a very long time, in a path called the water cycle. First, the sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and puddles. Some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. This is called evaporation. High in the sky, the air is cooler. There the vapor cools and turns back into tiny drops of water. Millions of drops gather to form clouds. When the drops join together and get too heavy, they fall as rain, or as snow if it is cold enough. The water runs into streams, soaks into the ground, or flows back to the sea. Then the sun warms it, and the cycle starts again.

q.text: What makes water turn into vapor?
q.why: "The sun warms water ... Some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapor."

q.text: What is evaporation?
c: water turning into a gas and rising into the air
q.why: "Some of it turns into an invisible gas ... and rises into the air. This is called evaporation."

q.text: Why does rain fall out of a cloud?
c: The sun pushes the drops down.
The drops join together and get too heavy.
q.why: "When the drops join together and get too heavy, they fall as rain."

q.text: What is this passage mostly about?
c: how clouds turn into snow in the winter
how water keeps moving between sea, sky, and land
how to save water at home
q.why: It follows water from the sea, up into clouds, down as rain, and back again — "the same water over and over."

ra_g4_09.title: A Bird in the Garage
ra_g4_09.text: When Owen opened the side door of the garage, a small brown sparrow zipped inside. It flew in frantic circles, bumping into the windows again and again. Owen's little sister grabbed a broom to chase it out. "Wait," Owen said. "Chasing it will only scare it more." He remembered reading that a frightened bird flies toward the brightest light. So he switched off the garage light and pulled the big door all the way up. Then the two of them sat on the steps and stayed perfectly still. For a few minutes, the sparrow rested on a high shelf, its tiny chest moving fast. At last it spotted the bright opening. With a quick flutter, it shot out into the sunny yard and landed in the maple tree. Owen's sister grinned. "Being quiet worked better than the broom," she said.

q.text: "It flew in frantic circles." What does frantic mean?
q.why: The bird was scared and kept "bumping into the windows again and again."

q.text: Why did Owen switch off the garage light?
c: so he could see the bird better
so the bird would go to sleep
so the open door would be the brightest place
so his sister would stop chasing
q.why: He knew "a frightened bird flies toward the brightest light," and then he opened the big door.

q.text: Where did the sparrow go when it left?
q.why: "It shot out into the sunny yard and landed in the maple tree." The shelf was inside, before it left.

q.text: What lesson does Owen's sister learn?
c: A broom is the best way to move a bird.
Staying calm can work better than chasing.
q.why: She says, "Being quiet worked better than the broom."

ra_g4_10.title: The Old Oak Speaks
ra_g4_10.text:
I stand at the edge of the meadow,
And I'm older than anyone here.
Inside me I keep all my birthdays,
A ring of new wood every year.

In spring I put on a green jacket.
The robins build nests on my arms.
In summer I lend you my shadow
To keep you from sunburn and harm.

In autumn I drop my whole jacket
In russet and copper and red,
And you leap in the piles that I give you
And laugh as they rain on your head.

In winter I stand bare and quiet.
I sleep through the snow and the storm,
But I dream of the spring and the robins
And wait for the days to grow warm.

So come and sit under my branches,
And bring me a story or two.
I've listened for two hundred summers,
But I'm happy to hear something new.

q.text: Who is speaking in this poem?
q.why: The speaker has rings of wood, robins nesting on its "arms," and drops leaves — it is the oak in the title.

q.text: What is the tree's "green jacket"?
c: a coat a child left there
q.why: It puts the jacket on in spring and drops it in autumn "in russet and copper and red" — the colors of fall leaves.

q.text: What does the tree give in summer?
q.why: "In summer I lend you my shadow / To keep you from sunburn."

q.text: What do the lines about rings tell you?
c: Trees wear rings on their branches.
Every tree is the same age.
You can tell a tree's age by its rings.
q.why: "I keep all my birthdays, / A ring of new wood every year." One ring for each year.

ra_g4_11.title: The Plant Doctor
ra_g4_11.text: George Washington Carver was born into slavery in Missouri around 1864. As a boy, he was so good with plants that neighbors called him "the plant doctor." He worked hard for years to go to school. He became a scientist. In 1896, he began to teach at a college in Alabama called Tuskegee. Many farmers there grew only cotton. The cotton wore out the soil. Carver showed them how to switch crops, planting peanuts or sweet potatoes in some years. Peanuts put nutrients, the things plants need to grow, back into the soil. Then he found new ways to use these crops. He made foods, dyes, and more. Carver had deep faith. He said that when he studied plants, he was learning about what God had made. He often got up before dawn to walk in the woods and pray.

q.text: What did his neighbors call him when he was a boy?
q.why: "... neighbors called him 'the plant doctor.'"

q.text: What are nutrients?
c: the things plants need to grow
q.why: The passage tells you: "nutrients, the things plants need to grow."

q.text: Why did Carver tell farmers to plant peanuts some years?
c: Cotton was too hard to pick.
Growing only cotton had worn out the soil.
q.why: "The cotton wore out the soil ... Peanuts put nutrients, the things plants need to grow, back into the soil."

q.text: What is the main idea?
c: Peanuts are the best food a farm can grow.
Most farmers in Alabama grew only cotton.
Carver liked to walk in the woods before dawn.
Carver, a man of deep faith, helped farmers save their soil.
q.why: He helped farmers save their soil and found new uses for crops; his faith shaped how he saw his work.

ra_g5_01.title: Why Ice Floats
ra_g5_01.text: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and it bobs at the top. That may not seem strange, but it is. Most substances shrink when they freeze, so the solid is heavier for its size than the liquid, and it sinks. Water is different. When water freezes, its tiny particles lock into a pattern with lots of open space. That makes ice take up more room than the water it came from. It is also why a glass bottle full of water can crack in the freezer. Because ice is lighter for its size than liquid water, it floats. This unusual fact matters a great deal to living things. In winter, ice forms on top of a lake and acts like a lid. It helps hold in warmth, so the water below stays liquid. Fish, frogs, and turtles can live through the winter in the cold water under the ice.

q.text: "Most substances shrink when they freeze." What are substances?
q.why: The passage compares water with other materials that freeze — "most substances."

q.text: Which detail supports the idea that ice takes up more room than the water it came from?
c: Fish can live under the ice.
A glass bottle full of water can crack in the freezer.
Ice forms on top of a lake.
Most substances shrink when they freeze.
Frogs and turtles live in lakes.
q.why: The bottle cracks because the freezing water needs more room than the bottle has.

q.text: Why can fish live through the winter in a frozen lake?
c: Fish leave the lake in winter.
The ice stays on top, so the water below stays liquid.
The sun melts the ice every day.
The ice sinks to the bottom.
q.why: Ice "acts like a lid" and "the water below stays liquid."

q.text: Why does the author write, "That may not seem strange, but it is"?
c: to warn readers that ice cubes can crack their glasses
to tell the reader to stop using ice
to make the reader curious about something they usually do not notice
to show that the author is confused
to explain how to make ice cubes
q.why: Everyone has seen ice float; the line gets the reader wondering why, before the passage explains.

ra_g5_02.title: Make a Needle Compass
ra_g5_02.text: Long before phones had maps, sailors found their way with compasses. You can make a simple one at home. You will need a sewing needle, a strong magnet, a small bowl of water, and a piece of cork or a flat leaf. Ask a grown-up to help, since the needle is sharp. First, stroke the needle with one end of the magnet about thirty times. Always rub in the same direction, from the eye of the needle to the point, lifting the magnet away before each new stroke. This turns the needle into a weak magnet. Next, lay the needle on the cork and float it in the middle of the bowl. Keep the bowl away from metal objects. Watch as the cork slowly turns. When it stops, the needle will point north and south. This works because Earth acts like a giant magnet, and your magnetized needle lines up with it.

q.text: What should the bowl be kept away from?
q.why: "Keep the bowl away from metal objects."

q.text: What does magnetized mean in these steps?
q.why: Stroking the needle "turns the needle into a weak magnet" — your "magnetized needle."

q.text: Why do you float the needle instead of laying it on a table?
c: so it can turn freely and line up north and south
so it does not get lost
to make it a stronger magnet
q.why: On the water "the cork slowly turns" until the needle points north and south. On a table it could not turn.

q.text: Why does the author begin with sailors?
c: to explain how to build a boat
to show that compasses have long helped people find their way
to warn that phones do not work at sea
to tell a story about a shipwreck
to show that sailors liked sewing
q.why: The first sentence introduces what a compass is for, before the steps.

ra_g5_03.title: The Paper Bridge
ra_g5_03.text: At science club, Ms. Ortiz handed each team one sheet of paper and a cup of pennies. "Build a bridge between these two books," she said. "The bridge that holds the most pennies wins." Theo laid his paper flat across the gap, but when he set down a single penny, the paper sagged right to the table. His partner, Imani, picked the paper back up and studied it. Then she folded it back and forth, like a fan, until it was full of sharp pleats. When she laid it across the books, it looked almost the same, but it was much stiffer. Theo added pennies one by one: ten, twenty, thirty, and still the bridge held. "How is that possible?" he asked. "The folds make it hard to bend," Imani said. "Each pleat is like a little wall standing on its edge." Their bridge finally sagged at forty-three pennies, the highest total in the entire club. On the way home, Theo noticed the wavy layer inside a torn cardboard box, and he smiled. Now he knew why it was there.

q.text: "Until it was full of sharp pleats." What are pleats?
q.why: She "folded it back and forth, like a fan, until it was full of sharp pleats."

q.text: How many pennies did the folded bridge hold before it sagged?
q.why: "Their bridge finally sagged at forty-three pennies." At thirty it was still holding.

q.text: Why did Theo smile at the cardboard box?
c: He saw that its wavy layer makes it strong, like the folds.
It was the box the club's pennies came in.
He was glad to be home.
It reminded him to buy more paper.
q.why: He had just learned that folds make paper "hard to bend." "Now he knew why it was there."

q.text: What is the main idea of the story?
c: Pennies are heavier than they look.
Theo is better at science than Imani.
Folding paper can make it much stronger.
q.why: Flat paper held one penny; folded paper held forty-three. The ending connects the idea to cardboard.

ra_g5_04.title: Follow the Blazes
ra_g5_04.text: Halfway up the mountain trail, Ella realized she could not see her family anymore. She had stopped to look at a salamander under a log, and now the path split in two directions. Her heart pounded. Then she remembered what her mother had told her that morning: "If you ever get separated, stay calm. If you can see the blazes, follow them. If you can't, stay right where you are." A blaze is a painted mark on a tree that shows hikers where the trail goes. Ella looked at the trees around her. On the left path, she saw nothing but bark. On the right, a bright blue rectangle was painted on an oak at eye level. Farther on, she could see another blue mark. Ella took a deep breath and followed the blue blazes, one tree at a time. Ten minutes later, she heard her brother shouting her name. Her family was waiting at a lookout, and her mother hugged her tight. "You found us," she said. "No," Ella said, grinning. "The trees did."

q.text: In this story, what is a blaze?
c: a painted mark on a tree that shows the trail
q.why: The story says: "A blaze is a painted mark on a tree that shows hikers where the trail goes."

q.text: Why did Ella fall behind her family?
c: She stopped to look at a salamander.
q.why: "She had stopped to look at a salamander under a log."

q.text: Why did Ella choose the right-hand path?
c: She heard her brother on that side.
It had blue marks on the trees, and the left one had none.
Her mother had told her to always go right.
q.why: "On the left path, she saw nothing but bark. On the right, a bright blue rectangle."

q.text: Which sentence best shows that Ella stayed calm?
c: She had stopped to look at a salamander under a log.
Ten minutes later, she heard her brother shouting her name.
Ella took a deep breath and followed the blue blazes, one tree at a time.
q.why: Taking a deep breath and going "one tree at a time" is calm, careful action. "Her heart pounded" shows the opposite.

ra_g5_05.title: Counting the Thunder
ra_g5_05.text: The lights flickered once, then went out. In the sudden darkness, Mateo's little brother grabbed his arm, and outside, rain hammered against the windows. "It's okay, Sam," Mateo said, switching on a flashlight. "Want to know a trick for telling how far away the storm is?" Sam nodded. "When you see lightning, start counting seconds. Stop when you hear the thunder." A white flash lit the room. "One, two, three," they counted together. On eleven, the thunder rumbled. "Light travels much faster than sound," Mateo explained. "We see the flash almost right away, but the sound takes about five seconds to go one mile. Eleven seconds means the lightning was about two miles away." They waited for the next flash, and this time they counted to fifteen. After the one that followed, they reached nineteen. Slowly, Sam's grip on Mateo's arm loosened. "It's getting farther away," he said. "Exactly," said Mateo. By the time the lights blinked back on, Sam was asleep on the couch, still holding the flashlight.

q.text: About how long does the sound of thunder take to travel one mile?
q.why: Mateo says "the sound takes about five seconds to go one mile."

q.text: Why did Sam's grip on Mateo's arm loosen?
c: He felt less scared as the storm moved away.
Mateo told him to let go.
The lights had come back on.
He wanted to count by himself.
q.why: It loosens right after the counts grow to fifteen and nineteen, and Sam says "It's getting farther away." The lights come on later.

q.text: Which detail best shows that the storm was moving away?
c: A white flash lit the room.
The counts went from eleven to fifteen to nineteen.
q.why: Longer counts mean the thunder took longer to arrive — so the lightning was farther off each time.

q.text: Why does the author include Mateo's explanation about light and sound?
c: to make the storm seem scarier
to show how the counting trick works
to explain why the lights went out
to tell how a flashlight works
to show that Mateo is bored
q.why: Without the explanation, the reader would not know why counting seconds tells the distance.

ra_g5_06.title: Follow the Brightest Sky
ra_g5_06.text: On summer nights along warm beaches, something small begins to stir in the sand. A nest of sea turtle eggs, buried by the mother about two months earlier, is hatching. Dozens of baby turtles, each small enough to fit in your palm, dig their way up to the surface. Then they must reach the ocean quickly, before crabs and birds find them. How do they know which way to go? The hatchlings head toward the brightest horizon. On a natural beach, that is the open sky over the water, which reflects light from the moon and stars. The land side, with its dunes and plants, looks darker. Today, though, many beaches are lined with houses, streetlights, and hotels. Bright lights on land can confuse the hatchlings and lead them away from the sea. That is why some beach towns ask people to turn off outdoor lights during nesting season. A darker beach helps more turtles find the water.

q.text: Which way do the hatchlings head?
q.why: "The hatchlings head toward the brightest horizon."

q.text: What is the horizon?
c: the line where the sky seems to meet the land or sea
q.why: "The brightest horizon ... is the open sky over the water" — where sky and sea meet.

q.text: Why might a hatchling crawl toward a parking lot?
c: It is looking for something to eat.
The parking lot lights look brighter than the sky over the sea.
It hears the cars and thinks they are waves.
The sand there is warmer than the beach.
q.why: Hatchlings go to the brightest place, and "bright lights on land can confuse the hatchlings."

q.text: What is the author's main purpose?
c: to tell a funny story about a turtle
to convince people to build more hotels
to explain why sea turtles bury their eggs in warm sand on summer nights
to explain how hatchlings find the sea and how lights can lead them the wrong way
q.why: The passage explains the hatchlings' trick, then the problem lights cause and what towns do about it.

ra_g5_07.title: A Sheep, a Duck, and a Rooster
ra_g5_07.text: In 1783, two French brothers, Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier, were testing a bold idea. They had noticed that smoke and heated air rise. Could that lift something large? The brothers ran a paper-making business, so they built a huge bag of cloth lined with paper. When they filled it with hot air from a fire, it floated up into the sky. But would it be safe for people? No one knew what the air high above the ground might do to a living creature. So in September 1783, in front of the king and queen of France and a huge crowd, the brothers sent up a balloon with a basket carrying three passengers: a sheep, a duck, and a rooster. The balloon flew for about eight minutes and came down a couple of miles away. All three animals landed alive. Two months later, two men rode a Montgolfier balloon over Paris. They became the first people to fly in a balloon that was not tied to the ground.

q.text: Who were the passengers on the September 1783 flight?
c: a sheep, a duck, and a rooster
q.why: "Three passengers: a sheep, a duck, and a rooster." The king and queen watched.

q.text: Why did the brothers send animals up before people?
c: because the animals were lighter than the brothers
because the king asked for farm animals
to find out if flying that high was safe for living things
because people were not allowed near fire
q.why: "Would it be safe for people? No one knew what the air ... might do to a living creature. So ..."

q.text: Why does the author mention that the king and queen were watching?
c: to show how important and public the test was
to explain who paid for the balloon
to show that the king rode in the balloon
to describe the weather that day
to tell where the animals came from
