q.why: A flight in front of the king, the queen and "a huge crowd" was a big public event.

q.text: What is the passage mostly about?
c: how the first hot-air balloons were tested and flown
the life of the king of France
q.why: It follows the balloon from the idea, to the animal test, to the first people flying.

ra_g5_08.title: The Long Flight of the Monarchs
ra_g5_08.text: Every fall, millions of monarch butterflies in eastern North America begin an amazing trip. They fly south to spend the winter in the mountain forests of central Mexico. Some travel about 3,000 miles. There they cluster on fir trees. So many crowd together that branches can bend under their weight. What makes this journey remarkable is that none of the butterflies has ever made it before. Most monarchs live only a few weeks. But the ones born at the end of summer are different. They can live for about eight months. That is long enough to fly to Mexico, rest through the winter, and start back north in spring. On the way, they lay eggs on milkweed. It is the only plant monarch caterpillars eat. Their children and grandchildren carry on the trip north. So the monarchs that fly to Mexico the next fall are the great-grandchildren, or even great-great-grandchildren, of the ones that left.

q.text: What is the only plant monarch caterpillars eat?
q.why: "They lay eggs on milkweed. It is the only plant monarch caterpillars eat." The fir trees are where the adults rest.

q.text: "What makes this journey remarkable" — what does remarkable mean?
c: unusual enough to be noticed and talked about
q.why: The author goes on to show what is surprising about the trip — no butterfly has made it before.

q.text: Which detail best supports the claim that the journey is remarkable?
c: Most monarchs live only a few weeks.
The forests are in central Mexico.
None of the butterflies has ever made the trip before.
q.why: The passage says this is "what makes this journey remarkable."

q.text: Why can the late-summer monarchs make the trip when others cannot?
c: They are bigger than other monarchs.
They do not need to eat.
They ride on the wind the whole way.
They live much longer than other monarchs.
They have made the trip before.
q.why: "Most monarchs live only a few weeks," but these "can live for about eight months. That is long enough to fly to Mexico."

ra_g5_09.title: Double the Recipe
ra_g5_09.text: Eight people were coming for breakfast, and Nadia's pancake recipe only made enough for four. "Just double everything," her grandfather said. Nadia copied the recipe onto a card and worked it out: 1 cup of flour became 2 cups, 1 egg became 2 eggs, and 3/4 cup of milk became 1 and 1/2 cups. She was careful with every line. But when she poured the batter onto the hot pan, it cooked up thin and flat as a coaster. Something was wrong. Nadia checked the card again. She had doubled the flour, the eggs, and the milk, but she had skipped one line. The recipe called for 2 teaspoons of baking powder, so she needed 4, and she had only added 2. "Baking powder makes tiny bubbles that puff pancakes up," Grandpa said. "Without enough, they stay flat." Nadia stirred in two more teaspoons. The next pancake rose tall and fluffy. After breakfast, she drew a box around the baking powder line so she would never miss it again.

q.text: How much baking powder did the doubled recipe need?
q.why: "The recipe called for 2 teaspoons of baking powder, so she needed 4."

q.text: Why were the first pancakes flat?
c: There was not enough baking powder to make bubbles.
Grandpa stirred the batter too hard.
q.why: She had added only 2 of the 4 teaspoons, and Grandpa says "Without enough, they stay flat."

q.text: Why does the author have Grandpa explain what baking powder does?
c: to show that Grandpa is a chef
to give the reader a new recipe
to explain why the guests came
so the reader understands why the pancakes stayed flat
q.why: His line connects the missing baking powder to the flat pancakes.

q.text: What lesson does the story show?
c: When you double a recipe, you must double every ingredient.
It is best to cook for only four people.
Milk is the most important ingredient.
q.why: Nadia doubled everything except one line, and that one line spoiled the first pancakes.

ra_g5_10.title: Snakes Are Out on the Trail
ra_g5_10.text:
NOTICE FROM THE PINE CREEK PARK RANGERS

Warm weather is here, and so are our snakes! Snakes are cold-blooded, which means their bodies warm up from the air and sun around them. That is why you may see them resting on sunny rocks or crossing the trail on warm days. Most snakes in North Carolina are harmless, and they help the park by eating mice and insects. However, a few kinds, such as the copperhead, are venomous, which means their bite carries venom, a kind of poison. Because it can be hard to tell one snake from another, please follow these rules for every snake you see. Stay on the trail, and watch where you put your hands and feet. Never try to touch, catch, or move a snake. If one is on the path, stand still, step back slowly, and give it plenty of room. It is not chasing you; it only wants to get away. Thank you for helping keep our visitors and our snakes safe!

q.text: What is the main purpose of this notice?
c: to explain why snakes in the park eat mice and insects
to warn people to stay out of the park for the whole summer
to tell visitors how to stay safe around snakes and leave them alone
to teach visitors how to catch a snake without getting bitten
to describe what a copperhead looks like up close
q.why: It explains why snakes are out, then gives rules: stay on the trail, never touch one, step back and give it room.

q.text: Which detail supports the claim that snakes help the park?
c: They rest on sunny rocks on warm days.
Their bodies warm up from the air and sun.
They only want to get away from people.
q.why: "Most snakes in North Carolina are harmless, and they help the park by eating mice and insects."

q.text: What should you do if a snake is on the path?
c: Stand still, step back slowly, and give it room.
Run past it as fast as you can before it moves.
Move it off the path with a long stick.
Call to it softly like a pet.
Wait for it to chase you away.
q.why: "If one is on the path, stand still, step back slowly, and give it plenty of room."

q.text: "Snakes are cold-blooded." What does cold-blooded mean here?
c: They feel cold to the touch in every season of the year.
They only live where it snows.
They have no blood running through their bodies at all.
Their bodies warm up from the air and sun around them.
q.why: The notice explains it: "which means their bodies warm up from the air and sun around them."

ra_g5_11.title: The Runner Who Would Not Race on Sunday
ra_g5_11.text: Eric Liddell was one of the fastest runners in Scotland. In 1924, he was picked to run for Great Britain at the Olympic Games in Paris. His best race was the 100 meters. But when the plan for the games came out, the heats for that race were on a Sunday. The heats are the early races that decide who goes on to the final. Liddell was a Christian, and he kept Sunday as a day of rest and worship. So he decided not to run that race. Some people said he was letting his country down. Instead, he trained for the 400 meters. It was a longer race, not his usual event, and few people thought he could win it. In the final, he ran almost the whole way at top speed. He crossed the line first and set a new Olympic record. The next year, Liddell went back to China, where he had been born, to work as a teacher and missionary. He spent most of the rest of his life there, serving others.

q.text: Why did Liddell not run the 100 meters?
c: He thought the race was too short.
His coach would not let him run.
Its heats were on Sunday, his day of rest and worship.
He wanted to go to China first.
q.why: "The heats for that race were on a Sunday ... Liddell was a Christian, and he kept Sunday as a day of rest and worship."

q.text: What are heats in this passage?
c: races run on very hot days
the fastest runners on a team
the early races that decide who goes on to the final
the last race, where the winner gets a medal
exercises runners do to warm up
q.why: The passage tells you: "The heats are the early races that decide who goes on to the final."

q.text: Which detail best shows that the 400 meters was not expected to be his race?
c: He was one of the fastest runners in Scotland.
The games were held in Paris.
It was not his usual event, and few people thought he could win it.
He went back to China the next year.
q.why: "It was a longer race, not his usual event, and few people thought he could win it."

q.text: Why does the author tell about Liddell's work in China at the end?
c: to explain where the next Olympics were held
to show that he quit running because he was tired
to describe what the weather is like in China
to tell how fast he could run
to show his faith guided his whole life
q.why: Choosing not to race on Sunday, and then a life "serving others" as a missionary, come from the same faith.

ra_g6_01.title: The Keeper's Daughter
ra_g6_01.text: In the winter of 1880, twelve-year-old Clara lived with her father in the lighthouse on Gull Point. Every evening at sunset, he climbed the spiral stairs to light the great oil lamp. Every few hours through the night, he climbed again to trim its wick so the flame would burn bright and steady. Lighthouse keepers were nicknamed "wickies" for that reason. One January night, a storm roared in from the sea, and her father came down with a fever so high he could barely stand. "The light," he whispered. "Ships are out there." Clara had watched him a hundred times. She pulled on her coat, took the oil can and the scissors, and climbed the ninety-two steps. Wind rattled the glass around her. All night she climbed up and down, trimming the wick, wiping soot from the glass, and refilling the oil. Near dawn, through the rain, she saw the lantern of a fishing boat turn safely away from the rocks below. In the morning, her father, still pale, asked who had kept the light burning. Clara did not answer. She was already asleep at the kitchen table, her hands still black with soot.

q.text: Why were lighthouse keepers nicknamed "wickies"?
c: They trimmed the lamp's wick through the night.
q.why: "He climbed again to trim its wick ... Lighthouse keepers were nicknamed 'wickies' for that reason."

q.text: "Trim its wick" — what does trim mean here?
q.why: Clara used "the scissors" to trim — she cut the wick so the flame would burn "bright and steady."

q.text: Why does her father whisper, "Ships are out there"?
c: He wants Clara to go fishing.
Without the light, ships could hit the rocks in the storm.
He wants a doctor to come by boat.
q.why: A lighthouse warns ships away from danger, and at dawn a boat turns "safely away from the rocks below."

q.text: Which detail best shows that Clara's work mattered?
c: Wind rattled the glass around her.
Her hands were black with soot.
She fell asleep at the kitchen table.
She saw a fishing boat turn safely away from the rocks.
q.why: The boat turning away safely shows the light did its job because she kept it burning.

ra_g6_02.title: The Chess Clock
ra_g6_02.text: Jonah was the fastest chess player at the community center. He could make a move in two seconds, and he loved watching his opponents squirm as he slapped the button on the chess clock. But in the spring tournament, he lost his first three games, every one to a player who seemed slow and almost sleepy. After the third loss, Mr. Haddad, the club's oldest member, sat down beside him. "You played those games like you were trying to catch a bus," he said. "Your opponent wasn't faster than you. She was more patient." He set up the final position from Jonah's last game and pointed. "Your knight was in danger for four moves. You never noticed, because you never stopped to ask what she was planning." Jonah stared at the board and realized that Mr. Haddad was right. In his rush, he had only looked at his own attacks. For his next game, he made himself a rule: before every move, count to ten and ask, "What does my opponent want?" The clock ticked, and every ten seconds felt like forever. But forty minutes later, Jonah shook hands after his first win of the day, and he had not lost a single piece by accident.

q.text: What does Mr. Haddad mean when he says Jonah played "like you were trying to catch a bus"?
c: Jonah was late to the tournament.
q.why: He goes on: "Your opponent wasn't faster than you. She was more patient." Jonah was hurrying.

q.text: What rule did Jonah make for his next game?
c: Count to ten and ask what his opponent wants.
q.why: "Before every move, count to ten and ask, 'What does my opponent want?'"

q.text: Why does the author say every ten seconds "felt like forever"?
c: to show that the clock was broken
to show that the game was boring
to explain how chess clocks work
to show how hard it was for Jonah to slow down
to show that Jonah was losing
q.why: Jonah was used to moving in two seconds; waiting ten took real effort.

q.text: What lesson does Jonah learn?
c: Thinking about the other side can matter more than speed.
Fast players are the best players.
It is fine to lose pieces by accident.
q.why: He lost by rushing and won once he stopped to ask what his opponent wanted.

ra_g6_03.title: Backyard Neighbors
ra_g6_03.text: Ms. Banerjee gave the co-op class a project: in pairs, make a poster about a local animal. Noor was paired with Felix, and within five minutes they were arguing about which animal to choose. Noor wanted the red fox, because she had seen one at the edge of her yard. Felix wanted the box turtle, because one visited his family's garden every summer. Each of them had a list of reasons, and neither was willing to give in. Ms. Banerjee listened for a moment and then asked a single question. "What do the fox and the turtle have in common?" Both of them thought about it for a moment. "They both live near people's houses," Noor said slowly. "And they both get hit by cars sometimes," Felix added. Ms. Banerjee smiled and walked away. Noor and Felix looked at each other, and slowly a new idea began to take shape. By the end of class, they had a title: "Backyard Neighbors: Sharing Our Yards with Wild Animals." The fox went on the left side of the poster and the turtle on the right. In the middle, they listed tips: drive slowly on country roads, keep trash cans closed, and leave a brush pile in a corner of the yard. When they were done, Noor said the best part was that they had stopped arguing.

q.text: "What do the fox and the turtle have in common?" What does in common mean?
q.why: Their answers are things that are true of both animals: both live near houses, both get hit by cars.

q.text: Why did Ms. Banerjee walk away instead of choosing an animal for them?
c: She wanted them to work out the answer together.
She had to help another pair.
She thought the project was finished.
q.why: She "smiled and walked away" just before "slowly a new idea began to take shape" — she let them find it.

q.text: Which tip is on their poster?
c: build a fence around the yard
q.why: Any of the three tips is right: "drive slowly on country roads, keep trash cans closed, and leave a brush pile."

q.text: What is the main lesson of the story?
c: Foxes are more interesting than turtles.
Looking for what two ideas share can turn an argument into teamwork.
Teachers should always choose for students.
Posters should have only one animal.
It is best to work alone.
q.why: One question about what the animals share turns the argument into a poster about both.

ra_g6_04.title: Late Frost
ra_g6_04.text: For three weeks, Tessa had watched her tomato seedlings grow on the porch, and on Saturday she finally planted all twelve in the garden. That evening, while she was drying the dishes, her father checked the weather report and frowned. "Frost tonight," he said. "It could drop to thirty degrees by morning." Tessa's stomach sank. Young tomato plants are tender, and one hard frost can blacken their leaves and kill them. She couldn't dig them all up again in the dark. Then she remembered something her grandmother used to do on cold spring nights: cover the garden. Tessa gathered every old bedsheet and towel she could find. With a flashlight in one hand, she draped them over the seedlings and weighed the corners down with rocks so the wind could not pull them away. Her father brought out a few buckets to set upside down over the smallest plants. The next morning, the lawn sparkled white, and the birdbath wore a thin skin of ice. Tessa lifted the first sheet slowly, holding her breath. Underneath, the leaves were green and perfectly healthy. The sheets had trapped the warmth rising from the soil, and that had been just enough.

q.text: "Young tomato plants are tender." What does tender mean here?
q.why: The next words explain it: "one hard frost can blacken their leaves and kill them."

q.text: Why does Tessa hold her breath as she lifts the first sheet?
c: She is trying not to wake her father.
She is nervous about whether the plants survived.
She is cold from the ice.
q.why: She had worked all evening to save them and did not yet know if it had worked.

q.text: Which detail best shows that the night really did go below freezing?
c: Her father checked the weather report.
She held a flashlight in one hand.
The birdbath wore a thin skin of ice.
The seedlings grew on the porch for three weeks.
q.why: Water only turns to ice at freezing temperatures.

q.text: Which sentence best sums up the story?
c: Tessa's grandmother teaches her to grow tomatoes.
Tessa and her father dig up the garden at night.
When a frost threatens her new plants, Tessa covers them and saves them.
A frost kills all of Tessa's tomato plants.
Tessa learns how to read a weather report.
q.why: The problem is the frost; the solution is the sheets; the plants are "perfectly healthy."

ra_g6_05.title: The Real Reason for the Seasons
ra_g6_05.text: Many people believe that summer comes when Earth moves closer to the sun. It is a reasonable guess, but it is wrong. In fact, Earth is closest to the sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere. The real reason for the seasons is that Earth is tilted. Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis, and that axis leans to one side by about 23 degrees. As Earth travels around the sun during the year, the tilt stays pointed the same way in space. For part of the year, the northern half of Earth leans toward the sun. Sunlight hits it more directly and the days are longer, so it warms up. That is summer. Six months later, the northern half leans away. Sunlight arrives at a low slant, spreading its energy over a wider area, and the days are short. That is winter. Meanwhile, the southern half of Earth has the opposite season. When it is summer in Canada, it is winter in Argentina. So if you ever spend a December holiday at a sunny beach, you might be in Australia.

q.text: What is Earth's axis?
c: the path Earth takes around the sun
the imaginary line Earth spins around
q.why: "Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis."

q.text: Which fact shows that being close to the sun does NOT cause summer?
c: Earth is closest to the sun in early January, during northern winter.
The days are longer in summer.
Argentina is in the southern half of Earth.
Earth travels around the sun during the year.
q.why: If closeness caused summer, January would be summer in the north — but it is winter.

q.text: It is July. What season is it in Argentina?
q.why: July is summer in the north, and the passage says "When it is summer in Canada, it is winter in Argentina."

q.text: Why is winter colder, according to the passage?
c: Earth is farther from the sun.
The sun gives off less heat in winter.
Sunlight comes in at a low slant and the days are short.
q.why: "Sunlight arrives at a low slant, spreading its energy over a wider area, and the days are short."

ra_g6_06.title: The Map in the Drawer
ra_g6_06.text:
In the bottom drawer of Grandpa's desk,
under rubber bands and broken pencils,
there is a map so old it has turned the color of tea.
Its folds are as soft as cloth.

Someone drew this coast by hand.
Someone counted every bay,
inked a tiny anchor where the harbor was,
filled the bay with tiny numbers
that tell how deep the water was,
and wrote in curling letters, Shoals here, keep away.
I wonder if they were afraid of the water,
or in love with it, or both.

There are roads on this map that are highways now,
and villages that have grown into cities,
a lighthouse drawn as a tiny star,
and one small island that is not on any map I can find today.
Maybe the sea took it.
Maybe the mapmaker made a mistake.
Maybe it is still out there, waiting.

I fold the map along its tired lines
and put it back beneath the pencils.
Someday I will draw a map of my own,
of the creek, the hill, the hollow tree,
and someone I will never meet
will open it and wonder about me.

q.text: What are the map's "tired lines"?
c: the roads that are now highways
the old creases where it has been folded many times
q.why: "I fold the map along its tired lines" — the folds, which are already "as soft as cloth" from years of use.

q.text: Which line best shows that the map is very old?
c: under rubber bands and broken pencils,
inked a tiny anchor where the harbor was,
Someday I will draw a map of my own,
There are roads on this map that are highways now,
of the creek, the hill, the hollow tree,
q.why: Roads only become highways over a long time. The other lines do not tell how old the map is.

q.text: How does the speaker feel about the person who made the map?
q.why: The speaker keeps wondering: "I wonder if they were afraid of the water" and "Maybe the mapmaker made a mistake."

q.text: What idea does the poem end with?
c: Old maps should be thrown away.
A map we make today may make someone wonder about us later.
q.why: "Someone I will never meet / will open it and wonder about me" — just as the speaker wonders about the old mapmaker.

ra_g6_07.title: The Clever Octopus
ra_g6_07.text: The octopus may be the cleverest animal without a backbone. It has eight flexible arms lined with suckers that can both grip and taste. It has three hearts and blue blood. Most surprising of all, many of its nerve cells are not in its head but spread through its arms, so each arm can explore and react partly on its own. When it is threatened, an octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and jet away. Octopuses are also masters of disguise. Special cells in their skin let them change color and pattern in a fraction of a second. Some can even change the texture of their skin, turning it bumpy to look like rock or coral. Because an octopus has no bones, it can squeeze through any opening larger than its beak, the one hard part of its body. Scientists who study octopuses have watched them solve puzzles, unscrew jar lids to reach food, and tell different people apart. Octopuses in aquariums have even been known to slip out of their tanks. Yet for all their cleverness, most octopuses live only a year or two.

q.text: Where are many of the octopus's nerve cells?
q.why: "Many of its nerve cells are not in its head but spread through its arms."

q.text: "Change the texture of their skin" — what is texture?
c: how a surface feels, such as smooth or bumpy
q.why: The example tells you: "turning it bumpy to look like rock or coral."

q.text: Which detail best supports the claim that the octopus is clever?
c: It can solve puzzles and unscrew jar lids.
It lives only a year or two.
q.why: Solving puzzles and opening jars are signs of intelligence; hearts, blood and arms are just body facts.

q.text: Why can an octopus slip through a gap you might think is too small?
c: It has no bones, and only its small beak is hard.
Its suckers pull the gap wider.
q.why: "Because an octopus has no bones, it can squeeze through any opening larger than its beak."

ra_g6_08.title: Find the North Star
ra_g6_08.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, the night sky can show you which way is north, even without a compass. Here is how to find Polaris, the North Star. First, get away from bright lights if you can, and give your eyes several minutes to adjust to the dark. Next, look for the Big Dipper: seven bright stars shaped like a ladle with a long, bent handle. Depending on the season and the time of night, the Dipper may appear right side up, upside down, or standing on its handle, so be patient. Find the two stars that form the outer edge of the Dipper's cup, the side farthest from the handle. These are called the pointer stars. Imagine a line running from the bottom pointer star through the top one, and follow it about five times the distance between them. The star you reach, shining by itself, is Polaris. It is not the brightest star in the sky, but it is the most useful. While other stars slowly wheel across the sky during the night, Polaris barely seems to move, because it sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole. Face it, and you are facing north.

q.text: Which stars point the way to Polaris?
c: the two stars on the outer edge of the Dipper's cup
the stars in the Dipper's handle
the brightest stars in the sky
the stars closest to the moon
any two stars that are close together
q.why: "Find the two stars that form the outer edge of the Dipper's cup ... These are called the pointer stars."

q.text: "Give your eyes several minutes to adjust to the dark." What does adjust mean?
q.why: After a few minutes in the dark your eyes get used to it, and you can see more stars.

q.text: Why does the author mention that the Dipper may appear upside down?
c: to show that the Dipper is broken
so readers will not give up if it does not look the way they expect
to explain why Polaris looks brighter in some seasons
to prove that the stars are far away
q.why: "So be patient" — the Dipper turns during the year and the night, so it will not always look the same.

q.text: Why is Polaris more useful for finding north than other stars?
c: It stays almost still above the North Pole while other stars move.
It is the brightest star, so it is the easiest to see.
It is the closest star to Earth.
It is part of the Big Dipper's handle.
q.why: "While other stars slowly wheel across the sky ... Polaris barely seems to move." It is "not the brightest."

ra_g6_09.title: The Pony Express
ra_g6_09.text: In 1860, a letter from Missouri to California could take weeks by stagecoach or months by ship. A company decided to try something faster: the Pony Express. Young riders on swift horses carried mail in leather pouches. Their route crossed nearly 2,000 miles of prairie, desert, and mountains. Along the route stood a chain of stations, roughly ten to fifteen miles apart. At each one, a rider leaped from his tired horse onto a fresh one and galloped on, often in about two minutes. After many stations, a new rider took over. The riders rode day and night, in all kinds of weather. They could carry a letter across the West in about ten days. The service was thrilling, and its riders became famous. Yet the Pony Express lasted only about a year and a half. In October 1861, a telegraph line was finished across the country. Now a message could travel by wire in minutes instead of days. Almost overnight, the Pony Express was no longer needed, and it soon shut down. Today it is remembered as a bold experiment. It is also a reminder of how quickly new inventions can change the way people communicate.

q.text: About how far apart were the stations?
q.why: "A chain of stations, roughly ten to fifteen miles apart."

q.text: Why did riders change horses so often?
c: The horses belonged to different families.
The riders liked to try new horses.
The mail was too heavy for one horse to lift.
The law said horses could only go one mile.
A fresh horse could keep running fast.
q.why: The rider "leaped from his tired horse onto a fresh one and galloped on" — tired horses slow down.

q.text: Which detail best explains why the Pony Express ended?
c: Stations were ten to fifteen miles apart.
Riders carried mail in leather pouches.
A telegraph line could send a message in minutes.
The route crossed mountains and deserts.
q.why: "Now a message could travel by wire in minutes instead of days. Almost overnight, the Pony Express was no longer needed."

q.text: What is the author's main purpose in this passage?
c: to persuade readers to ride horses
to tell how the telegraph was invented
to explain what the Pony Express was and why it ended so soon
q.why: It describes how the Pony Express worked, then how the telegraph replaced it.

ra_g6_10.title: The Burr That Became a Fastener
ra_g6_10.text: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk in the mountains with his dog. When they got home, both of them were covered with burrs, the prickly seed heads of a plant called burdock. Pulling them off took a long time. Most people would have grumbled and thrown the burrs away, but de Mestral was curious. Why did they stick so well? He looked at one under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks. The hooks caught on anything with loops, like the threads of his socks or the fur of his dog. He wondered whether people could copy the idea. For years he experimented, trying one material after another. Cotton wore out too quickly, but a strong new material called nylon worked. He made one strip covered with tiny hooks and another covered with tiny loops. Pressed together, they held tight; pulled apart, they opened with a ripping sound. He patented his invention in the 1950s. Today, hook-and-loop fasteners close shoes, jackets, and backpacks, and astronauts have used them to keep tools from floating away. It all began with a curious man and a dog covered in burrs.

q.text: "For years he experimented." What does experimented mean?
c: tried different ways to see what worked
gave up on an idea after it failed once
walked a long way through the mountains
q.why: The sentence goes on: "trying one material after another." Cotton failed; nylon worked.

q.text: What did de Mestral see when he looked at a burr under a microscope?
q.why: "He looked at one under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks." The loops were on his socks and dog.

q.text: What can you tell about de Mestral from this passage?
c: He did not like his dog.
He was curious and kept trying for years.
He gave up as soon as the cotton wore out.
He was an astronaut who went to space.
q.why: He asked "Why did they stick so well?" when others would have grumbled, and "for years he experimented."

q.text: Why does the author mention that most people would have grumbled and thrown the burrs away?
c: to explain how to remove burrs
to warn readers to stay away from burdock plants
to show how unusual de Mestral's curiosity was
to show that de Mestral was grumpy
to explain why cotton wore out too quickly
q.why: It sets up the contrast: "but de Mestral was curious."

ra_g6_11.title: Walking Instead of Riding
ra_g6_11.text: In the 1950s, Martin Luther King Jr. was the young pastor of a Baptist church in Montgomery, Alabama. At that time, laws in many Southern states kept Black and white Americans apart. In Montgomery, Black riders had to sit at the back of city buses. When a bus was full, they had to give up their seats to white riders. In 1955, a woman named Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat. Black citizens decided to stop riding the buses. This kind of protest is called a boycott, and they chose King to lead it. For more than a year, thousands of people walked or shared rides to work instead. King's faith taught him to love even the people who treated him unfairly. So he insisted that the protest stay peaceful, with no violence in return. In 1956, the Supreme Court ruled that the bus law broke the Constitution, and the boycott ended. King went on to lead marches across the country. In 1963, he gave his famous "I Have a Dream" speech in the nation's capital. In 1964, he won the Nobel Peace Prize for working for change without violence.

q.text: What is a boycott, in this passage?
c: a protest where people stop using something
q.why: They "decided to stop riding the buses. This kind of protest is called a boycott."

q.text: Why did Black citizens choose to stop riding the buses?
c: to protest an unfair bus rule
because the buses were too slow
because King told them buses were unsafe
because the buses had stopped running
q.why: "Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat. Black citizens decided to stop riding the buses."

q.text: Which detail best shows that King's faith shaped how he led the protest?
c: He gave his famous "I Have a Dream" speech in the capital in 1963.
For more than a year, thousands of people walked or shared rides to work.
His faith taught him to love unfair people, so he kept the protest peaceful.
In 1956, the Supreme Court ruled against the bus law, and the boycott ended.
Black citizens chose him to lead the boycott after Rosa Parks was arrested.
q.why: The passage links the two: "King's faith taught him to love even the people who treated him unfairly. So he insisted that the protest stay peaceful."

q.text: How did the boycott end?
c: The buses stopped running for good.
Rosa Parks gave up her seat.
The Supreme Court ruled the bus law broke the Constitution.
The marchers got tired of walking.
q.why: "In 1956, the Supreme Court ruled that the bus law broke the Constitution, and the boycott ended."

ra_g78_01.title: Cities Built by Animals
ra_g78_01.text: A coral reef looks like a garden of colorful rocks and plants, but it is actually built by animals. Each reef-building coral is a colony of many tiny creatures called polyps. A polyp is soft, often no bigger than a pencil eraser, with a ring of stinging tentacles around its mouth. To protect itself, each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone beneath its body. When polyps die, their skeletons remain, and new polyps grow on top. Over thousands of years, these layers build up into huge reefs. The Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Australia, stretches for more than 1,400 miles. Many reef-building corals depend on a partnership. Tiny algae live inside the polyps. Using sunlight, the algae make food and share much of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe home. The algae also give many corals their color. This partnership is why most reefs grow in shallow, clear water. When the water stays too warm for too long, corals become stressed and push the algae out. Without them, the coral turns white, which is called bleaching. Bleached coral is not yet dead, but if the water does not cool down, it may starve. Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all known ocean species live on or around them.

q.text: What are polyps?
c: colorful rocks on the sea floor
the algae that live in coral
the tiny soft animals that build coral
q.why: "Each reef-building coral is a colony of many tiny creatures called polyps."

q.text: What gives many corals their color?
q.why: "The algae also give many corals their color." That is why bleached coral turns white.

q.text: Why do most reefs grow in shallow, clear water?
c: Polyps cannot swim in deep water.
Fish only live in shallow water.
The algae inside the coral need sunlight to make food.
Deep water is too cold for limestone.
Divers can protect them more easily.
q.why: The algae make food "using sunlight," and "this partnership is why most reefs grow in shallow, clear water."

q.text: Which detail best supports the idea that reefs are important to ocean life?
c: A polyp is often no bigger than a pencil eraser.
The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Australia.
About a quarter of all known ocean species live on or around them.
q.why: So many kinds of fish depending on such a small area shows how important reefs are.

ra_g78_02.title: The Last Ice Harvest
ra_g78_02.text: In January of 1938, when the ice on Miller's Pond had grown a foot thick, Henry's grandfather woke him well before dawn. "This will probably be the last harvest," Grandpa said, pulling on his boots. "Folks are buying electric refrigerators now, and before long nobody will need pond ice." Out on the pond, the men worked in a steady rhythm that seemed to Henry almost like a dance. First they scraped away the snow; then a horse dragged a sharp-bladed plow across the surface, cutting long, straight grooves in a grid. Men followed with long-toothed saws, finishing each cut until enormous blocks broke loose and floated in the black water. With an iron pole, Henry helped guide the blocks along an open channel toward the ice house on the shore. Inside, the blocks were stacked to the rafters and packed in thick layers of sawdust, which kept the warm air away so that the ice would last until August. Then Grandpa would deliver it, block by block, to the iceboxes in town. At noon, Henry sat on a sled eating a cold sandwich and watching his breath drift upward. He tried to memorize everything: the squeal of the saws, the steam rising from the horse's back, the faint blue glow inside each block. "Will you miss it?" he asked. Grandpa gazed at the gray rectangles of open water, which were already freezing over again. "I'll miss the work, but I won't miss the cold," he said. "Things change, Henry. The trick is remembering how they used to be."

q.text: What kept the ice from melting in the ice house?
q.why: "Packed in thick layers of sawdust, which kept the warm air away so that the ice would last until August."

q.text: "The men worked in a steady rhythm." What does rhythm mean here?
q.why: "Steady" and "almost like a dance" — the same jobs done over and over at an even pace.

q.text: Why does Henry try to memorize everything?
c: He has a test about ice the next day.
He knows this may be the last ice harvest.
He wants to become a horse trainer.
Grandpa asked him to write a report.
He plans to build his own ice house.
q.why: Grandpa said "This will probably be the last harvest," because refrigerators are replacing pond ice.

q.text: Why does the author have Grandpa mention electric refrigerators at the very start?
c: to explain why this harvest may be the last one
to show that Grandpa sells refrigerators
to describe how ice houses work
to make the morning seem warmer
to prove that Henry is lazy
q.why: It sets up the whole story: a way of life that is ending, which Henry wants to remember.

ra_g78_03.title: Build a Marble Roller Coaster
ra_g78_03.text: Most roller coasters have no engine pulling them along the track. Once it is dragged to the top of the first hill, gravity does the rest. You can see how this works by building a marble roller coaster at home. You will need foam pipe insulation from a hardware store, scissors, masking tape, a marble, and a cup. First, ask a grown-up to cut the foam tubes in half the long way, so that each one becomes two open tracks. Tape the end of one track high on a wall or the back of a chair. This is your first hill, and it must be the highest point of the whole ride. Tape more pieces together to make dips, smaller hills, and curves, ending in a cup on the floor. Now drop the marble at the top and watch where it slows down and where it speeds up. If it stops before the end, the problem is usually a hill that is too high. A marble can never climb back up as high as the point where it started, because some of its energy is always lost to friction, the rubbing between the marble and the track. Lower that hill, or raise your starting point, and try again. Real roller coaster designers solve the same puzzle, only with steel instead of foam. Engineers carefully calculate every hill and curve so that the cars always keep enough energy to reach the station at the end.

q.text: What is friction, in these steps?
c: the pull that makes the marble fall
the highest hill of the ride
the tape that holds the track
the rubbing between the marble and the track
q.why: The steps define it: "friction, the rubbing between the marble and the track."

q.text: What must be true of the first hill?
c: It must be the shortest piece of track in the ride.
It must be the highest point of the whole ride.
It must end in the cup.
It must have a curve in it.
It must be taped to the floor.
q.why: "This is your first hill, and it must be the highest point of the whole ride."

q.text: Your marble stops partway up the third hill. What should you try?
c: Put a heavier cup at the end of the track.
Lower that hill or raise the starting point.
Add more tape to the first hill.
Add more tape along the bottom of the third hill.
q.why: "If it stops before the end, the problem is usually a hill that is too high ... Lower that hill, or raise your starting point."

q.text: Why does the author begin by explaining that most roller coasters have no engine?
c: to show that gravity from the first hill powers the whole ride
to explain how the engines on real roller coasters work
to warn readers that roller coasters are unsafe
to describe the steel that real roller coasters are built from
to tell readers where to buy foam tubes
q.why: The model works the same way: once the marble is at the top, "gravity does the rest."

ra_g78_04.title: The Colony That Vanished
ra_g78_04.text: In 1587, about 115 English men, women, and children sailed across the Atlantic Ocean to start a settlement on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina. Their leader was an artist named John White. Soon after they arrived, his daughter gave birth to a girl named Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas. The colonists soon realized they would run short of supplies, so White sailed back to England for help, expecting to return within months. Instead, he was delayed for three years. England was at war with Spain, and nearly every ship was needed for the fight. When White finally returned in August 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down, and there was no sign of a battle. The only clues were letters carved into wood: CRO on a tree and the word CROATOAN on a post. Croatoan was the name of a nearby island and of the Native American people who lived there, who had been friendly to the English. White hoped the colonists had moved there, but a storm drove his ship back to England before he could search. No one knows for certain what happened to the colonists, and historians and archaeologists are still looking for answers today. That is why it is called the Lost Colony.

q.text: What word was carved on the post?
q.why: "CRO on a tree and the word CROATOAN on a post."

q.text: Why did White hope the colonists had gone to Croatoan?
c: He had told them to sail home to England without him.
He could see their houses standing on that island.
The carving named it, and the people there had been friendly.
The storm had already blown his ship onto that island.
q.why: The carved clue "CROATOAN" named a nearby island whose people "had been friendly to the English."

q.text: Which detail best supports the idea that the colonists were not attacked before they left?
c: White was delayed in England for three whole years.
England was at war with Spain.
A storm drove his ship back to England before he could search.
The houses had been taken down, and there was no sign of a battle.
Virginia Dare was born soon after they arrived.
q.why: "The houses had been taken down, and there was no sign of a battle" — which suggests the colonists left on purpose.

q.text: "Instead, he was delayed for three years." What does delayed mean?
c: lost at sea on the way back
made the leader of the colony
q.why: He meant to return "within months" but could not, because "nearly every ship was needed for the fight."

ra_g78_05.title: Field Notes
ra_g78_05.text: For her science project, Amara made a prediction: more birds would visit her feeder on colder days. The idea seemed obvious, since birds need extra energy to stay warm and should therefore eat more when temperatures drop below freezing. For three weeks, she sat by the kitchen window for twenty minutes every morning, recording the outdoor temperature and making a tally mark for every bird that landed on the feeder. When she finally organized her numbers into a chart, however, she frowned. Several of the coldest mornings had attracted very few visitors. On the most bitter morning of all, when the thermometer read eleven degrees, she had counted only four birds, yet a mild morning the following week had brought twenty-three. "My prediction was wrong," she told her uncle, a biologist who studied birds for a living. "The whole project is ruined." Her uncle paged thoughtfully through her notebook. "Wrong isn't ruined," he said. "Look at your notes about the weather, not just the temperature." Amara examined the pages again and noticed that beside each of the busiest days, she had written the same word: snow. On those mornings, fresh snow had blanketed the ground, hiding the seeds that birds normally find for themselves. On that eleven-degree morning, the coldest of all, the ground had been completely bare. "So it isn't really the cold," she said slowly. "It's whether they can find food anywhere else." Her uncle smiled. "Now you have a new question to test, and that is exactly how science is supposed to work."

q.text: What is a prediction?
c: a guess about what will happen, made before testing it
a final answer that has been proven
q.why: Amara made her prediction first, then spent three weeks testing it — and it turned out wrong.

q.text: Which detail best supports Amara's new idea about the birds?
c: She sat by the kitchen window for twenty minutes every morning.
Birds need extra energy to stay warm.
Her uncle studied birds for a living.
Beside each of the busiest days, she had written the same word: snow.
She made a tally mark for every bird that landed.
q.why: Her new idea is that snow hides the birds' natural food — and the busiest days were the snowy ones.

q.text: Why did only four birds come on the coldest morning?
c: It was too cold for birds to fly.
The ground was bare, so they could find food elsewhere.
Amara forgot to fill the feeder.
q.why: "On that eleven-degree morning, the coldest of all, the ground had been completely bare" — seeds were easy to find without the feeder.

q.text: What is the main message of the story?
c: Science projects should always prove the prediction right.
Birds do not need food in winter.
Uncles are better at science than students.
A prediction that turns out wrong can still lead to new discoveries.
Cold weather is the most important thing to measure.
q.why: "Wrong isn't ruined ... Now you have a new question to test, and that is exactly how science is supposed to work."

ra_g78_06.title: The Long Road to Paper
ra_g78_06.text: Look around and you will probably see paper everywhere: books, boxes, receipts, napkins. Yet for most of human history, paper did not exist. People pressed words into clay tablets, carved them into stone, or wrote on papyrus, made from strips of a reed pressed together, or on parchment, made from carefully prepared animal skin. These worked, but clay was heavy, papyrus became brittle and cracked, and parchment was expensive. Paper was first made in China about two thousand years ago. Early papermakers soaked plant fibers, such as tree bark, hemp, and old rags, and beat them into a soggy pulp. They spread the pulp thinly on a screen, let the water drain away, and dried the thin mat that was left. The result was light, cheap, and easy to write on. For centuries, papermaking stayed mostly in East Asia. Gradually, the knowledge traveled west along trade routes, reaching the Middle East by the 700s and Europe several centuries later. For a long time, most paper in Europe was made from old cloth rags. In the 1800s, the demand for paper grew so large that there were not enough rags, and inventors found ways to make paper from wood. That change made paper cheap enough for newspapers, school notebooks, and eventually the boxes and bags we use today. Every sheet still follows the basic recipe of those early papermakers: fibers, water, a screen, and patience.

q.text: "Beat them into a soggy pulp." What is pulp?
c: a soft, wet mass of mashed fibers
q.why: Fibers are soaked and beaten until soggy, then the pulp is spread on a screen to dry into paper.

q.text: What did papermakers in the 1800s start using when there were not enough rags?
q.why: "There were not enough rags, and inventors found ways to make paper from wood."

q.text: Which sentence best states the main idea?
c: Clay was heavy, papyrus cracked, and parchment cost too much for most people.
Parchment was made from carefully prepared animal skin.
Paper, first made in China, slowly spread around the world and became cheap enough for everyday use.
In the 1800s, inventors found a way to make paper from wood instead of rags.
Paper reached the Middle East by the 700s and Europe several centuries later.
q.why: The passage traces paper from its start in China, across the world, to cheap wood paper. The others are single details.

q.text: Why does the author end with "fibers, water, a screen, and patience"?
c: to show that paper today is still made the same basic way as long ago
to give a list of things to buy
to prove that papermaking is too hard
to tell readers to be patient when reading
q.why: The final sentence links today's paper back to "the basic recipe of those early papermakers."

ra_g78_07.title: The Toughest Animal on Earth
ra_g78_07.text: If you scooped up a clump of damp moss and looked at it under a microscope, you might find one of the toughest animals on Earth. Tardigrades, also called water bears, are usually less than a millimeter long. They have plump bodies and eight stubby legs tipped with claws, and they lumber along like tiny bears. They live almost everywhere: in moss and soil, in ponds and oceans, from mountaintops to the deep sea. What makes tardigrades famous is their ability to survive conditions that would kill nearly any other animal. When their home dries out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs, loses almost all the water in its body, and curls into a dry little ball called a tun. In this state, its body nearly stops working. A tardigrade in a tun can survive being frozen and huge doses of radiation. In 2007, scientists sent dried tardigrades into orbit on the outside of a spacecraft, exposed to the emptiness of space. When the tardigrades came back to Earth and were given water, some of them revived and later laid eggs. Tardigrades are not invincible, however. In their active, everyday state, they are much more fragile, and they need a thin film of water around them to move, eat, and breathe. Their toughness is a survival trick for hard times, not a superpower they use all the time.

q.text: What does a tardigrade do when its home dries out?
c: It curls into a dry ball called a tun.
It digs deep into the soil.
q.why: "It pulls in its legs, loses almost all the water in its body, and curls into a dry little ball called a tun."

q.text: "Tardigrades are not invincible." What does invincible mean?
q.why: The next sentence contrasts it: in everyday life "they are much more fragile."

q.text: Which detail best supports the claim that tardigrades are extremely tough?
c: Some revived and laid eggs after being exposed to space.
They are usually less than a millimeter long.
They are also called water bears.
They live everywhere from mountaintops to the deep sea.
q.why: Surviving the emptiness of space is the strongest evidence; the others only describe them.

q.text: Why does the author end by calling their toughness "a survival trick, not a superpower"?
c: to suggest that tardigrades have superpowers
to explain how to find tardigrades
to correct the idea that tardigrades can survive anything at any time
to compare tardigrades with real bears
to warn readers that tardigrades are dangerous
q.why: The last part shows they are "much more fragile" when active — the toughness only works in the tun state.

ra_g78_08.title: The Fix-It Fair
ra_g78_08.text: Ezra's grandmother had owned her brass reading lamp for forty years, so when it flickered and finally died, she flatly refused to throw it away. "There's a fix-it fair at the library on Saturday," she announced. "Let's see what they can do." Ezra pictured rides and cotton candy, but the library's meeting room turned out to be crowded with folding tables, each staffed by a volunteer with a well-worn toolbox. At one table, a woman was carefully stitching the torn strap of a backpack; at another, a man was gluing the wobbly leg of an antique wooden chair. At the electrical table, a retired engineer named Mr. Osei waved them over and, before doing anything else, pulled the lamp's plug from the wall. "First rule," he explained. "Never work on anything that is connected to electricity." He invited Ezra to help, and together they eliminated the simplest possibilities first, replacing the bulb and then testing the switch, without any success. Finally, Mr. Osei unscrewed the base and revealed two thin copper wires, one of which had worked itself loose from its screw. "Forty years of being switched on and off," he said. "Eventually, things wiggle." He let Ezra wrap the wire around the screw and tighten it, and when they plugged the lamp back in, it glowed a warm, steady gold. On the walk home, Ezra kept thinking about how many appliances his family had discarded simply because they had stopped working, when the problem might have been something as small as a loose wire. "Next month," he said, "can we bring the toaster?"

q.text: Based on the story, what is a fix-it fair?
c: a store that sells new lamps
an event where volunteers help people fix broken things
a place to throw old things away
q.why: The room was "crowded with folding tables, each staffed by a volunteer with a well-worn toolbox," fixing a backpack, a chair and a lamp.

q.text: What was wrong with the lamp?
c: A wire had come loose from its screw.
q.why: "One of which had worked itself loose from its screw." The new bulb and the switch were tried first, "without any success."

q.text: Why did Mr. Osei and Ezra test the bulb and switch first?
c: They are the simplest and most common things to check.
They are the most expensive parts.
Mr. Osei did not know how to open the base.
q.why: "Together they eliminated the simplest possibilities first." You rule out easy problems before taking the lamp apart.

q.text: Why does the author describe the woman sewing a backpack and the man gluing a chair?
c: to explain how to sew a backpack
to show that many kinds of things get fixed at a fix-it fair
to show that the library was too crowded
to show that Mr. Osei was busy
q.why: These details show Ezra (and the reader) what a fix-it fair is, before the lamp is fixed.

ra_g78_09.title: Save the Climbing Tree
ra_g78_09.text:
To the Town Parks Board:

I am writing about the plan to cut down the big oak tree by the playground in Hillcrest Park so that the parking lot can be made larger. I understand why the board believes additional parking is necessary. On busy weekends, families circle the lot for a long time, and I know that is frustrating. However, cutting down the oak would be a mistake. First, the oak is part of what makes the park special. Kids have climbed its low branches for generations, and my grandfather has a photo of himself in it when he was ten. Second, the tree keeps the playground cool. On a July afternoon last summer, I measured the slide in full sun at 122 degrees, too hot to touch, while the slide in the oak's shade was 88. Third, there is a practical alternative that should satisfy everyone. The empty grass lot across Elm Street could hold twenty more cars, and the town already owns it. Some people say the oak is old and could drop a branch on someone. That is a fair worry, but the answer is to have a tree expert check it and trim any weak limbs, not to cut down the whole tree. A tree like this takes a lifetime to grow and a single afternoon to remove. I urge the board to keep the climbing tree and build the extra parking across the street.

Sincerely,
A Hillcrest Park neighbor

q.text: What is the writer's main purpose?
c: to explain how to measure the temperature of a slide
to complain about families who drive to the park
to persuade the board to keep the oak and add parking across the street
to describe the history of Hillcrest Park and its oldest trees
to ask the town to tear down the old playground and build a new one
q.why: The letter ends: "I urge the board to keep the climbing tree and build the extra parking across the street."

q.text: Which detail best supports the claim that the tree keeps the playground cool?
c: Kids have climbed its low branches for many generations.
The empty grass lot across Elm Street could hold twenty more cars.
The slide in the sun was 122 degrees, but the slide in the shade was 88.
On busy weekends, families circle the lot for a long time.
A tree expert could trim any weak limbs.
q.why: The two measurements compare sun and shade — direct evidence about cooling.

q.text: Why does the writer mention that some people worry the oak could drop a branch?
c: to agree that the tree should be cut down
to show that the writer is afraid of the tree
to change the subject to parking
to answer a worry from the other side
to prove that the oak is very young
q.why: The writer states the worry, calls it fair, and then answers it: have an expert "check it and trim any weak limbs."

q.text: Where does the writer say the extra parking could go?
c: the empty grass lot across Elm Street
in the space under the old oak tree
in the lot behind the town library
q.why: "The empty grass lot across Elm Street could hold twenty more cars, and the town already owns it."

ra_g78_10.title: The Honest Speech
ra_g78_10.text: The election for president of the Young Naturalists Club came down to two candidates: Marisol and a confident boy named Grant. Grant spoke first, and his speech was a crowd-pleaser. He promised a field trip to the aquarium every month, a pizza party after every meeting, and a free club T-shirt for every member, and the room erupted in applause. Marisol looked down at her own notes. She had planned to promise monthly trips as well, but the night before, she had examined the club's budget and discovered that it held barely enough money for two trips in the entire year. When her turn came, she took a deep breath and set her notes aside. "I'd love to promise you pizza and aquariums," she said, "but I looked carefully at our budget, and we simply can't afford them. If I promised those things, I would be breaking that promise by March." A few members groaned. "Here is what I can honestly promise," she continued. "One major trip in the spring, which we will choose together; a bake sale to raise money for a second trip; and meetings where we actually go outside, beginning with a creek study next month and a bird count in February." When the votes were counted, Grant had won by six. Marisol was disappointed, but she offered to help him with the planning anyway. By December, the club treasury was empty and the monthly trips had stopped. That same week, three members quietly asked Marisol whether she would consider running again next year.

q.text: Grant's speech "was a crowd-pleaser." What does that mean?
c: Many people in the audience enjoyed it.
It was about crowds of animals.
Only a few people heard it.
q.why: Right after his promises, "the room erupted in applause."

q.text: Why did Marisol set her notes aside?
c: She had forgotten what she wanted to say.
She chose to be honest about the budget instead.
She had decided to copy Grant's promises instead.
She was giving up the election.
Her notes were about a different club.
q.why: Her notes promised monthly trips, but she had learned the budget could not pay for them, so she spoke honestly instead.

q.text: Which detail best shows that Marisol's warning was correct?
c: Marisol was disappointed, but she offered to help him with the planning.
By December, the club treasury was empty and the monthly trips had stopped.
q.why: She said the promises would be broken "by March"; in fact the money ran out even sooner.

q.text: Which statement best expresses the theme of the story?
c: The most popular speech always wins.
Clubs should never take field trips.
Pizza parties are the key to a good club.
Honest promises may lose at first but can earn trust over time.
It is unwise to help someone who beat you.
q.why: Marisol loses the vote, but after Grant's promises fail, members come back to her.

ra_g78_11.title: The March to the Sea
ra_g78_11.text: Mohandas Gandhi was born in India in 1869, when India was ruled by Britain. As a young lawyer working in South Africa, he was thrown off a train for sitting in a first-class seat that was kept for white passengers, even though he had a ticket. The experience changed the direction of his life. Gandhi was a Hindu, and his faith taught a principle called ahimsa, which means doing no harm to any living thing. He came to believe that people could resist unfair laws without violence: by openly and peacefully refusing to obey them, and by accepting the punishment that followed. Back in India, he led millions of people in this kind of protest. Under British law, it was illegal for Indians to make their own salt, and the salt they bought was taxed. In 1930, Gandhi set out on foot from his home toward the sea, a walk of about 240 miles. Thousands of people joined him along the way. When he reached the coast, he picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore, breaking the law with one simple, peaceful act. People across India followed his example, and tens of thousands were jailed. India finally became independent in 1947.
